questions.stem: An attacker floods an inference endpoint with long, complex prompts that exhaust GPU memory and crash every tenant's instances. Which control addresses this availability threat?
options: Fine-tuning the model with LoRA so it produces shorter, cheaper outputs
k-anonymity masking applied to the incoming prompts
Semantic DLP filtering on each prompt and response
Compute throttling, execution timeouts and token rate limits
questions.explanation: Resource exhaustion is countered by limiting how much compute, time and how many tokens any client can consume. DLP and k-anonymity address data exposure, not availability.

questions.stem: During a forensic investigation of suspected training data poisoning, what must be preserved to reconstruct how the attack happened?
options: Model checkpoints, dataset version hashes, training configuration and ingestion logs
Badge access logs for the data center racks that host the training cluster
The compiler version that was used to build the pipeline's Python dependencies
The final responses shown to end users during the period of the suspected attack, exported from the chat interface
questions.explanation: Reconstructing a poisoning attack means showing when and how bad data entered the pipeline and which model versions absorbed it. That requires checkpoints, immutable dataset hashes, training configuration and ingestion logs.

references.chapterTitle: Operational Resilience: Monitoring, Incident Response, and Continuous Improvement
references.section: Investigation and analysis techniques for LLM incidents

questions.stem: A critical remote code execution flaw is disclosed in an open-source library used by model-serving pipelines. Which records best show where it's deployed so patching can be prioritized?
options: The ISC2 Code of Ethics and the organization's AI policy
The model vulnerability register and the AI bill of materials
The transparency disclosures published under the EU AI Act
The privacy impact assessments completed for each AI system before deployment
questions.explanation: An AIBOM inventories the components and dependencies of each AI system, and the vulnerability register tracks exposure, owners and status. Together they show which deployments are affected and in what priority to patch.

questions.stem: Red teamers use multi-turn conversations to systematically bypass a model's safety guardrails and elicit prohibited content. What kind of testing is this?
options: Verification of data sovereignty and residency compliance
Static application security testing of the model-serving code and its dependencies
Adversarial red teaming of generative AI, including jailbreak testing
Fuzzing the network socket buffers of the inference service
questions.explanation: Probing a generative model with adversarial prompts, including multi-turn escalation, to find safety and alignment failures is AI red teaming. SAST and fuzzing test code and interfaces, not model behavior.

questions.stem: A model learns to schedule data center cooling by trying settings and receiving a reward when energy use falls without overheating. Which learning paradigm is this?
options: Semi-supervised labeling
Supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Unsupervised clustering
questions.explanation: Learning through actions and rewards from an environment is reinforcement learning. Supervised learning needs labeled examples; clustering finds structure without a reward signal.

questions.stem: Which neural network architecture is most closely associated with image recognition because it learns spatial features through filters?
options: Transformer decoder used for text
Recurrent neural network (RNN)
Autoencoder used for compression
Convolutional neural network (CNN)
questions.explanation: CNNs apply learned filters across an image to detect edges, textures and shapes. Transformers now also handle images, but CNNs are the classic spatial-feature architecture.

questions.stem: What mechanism lets a transformer weigh how relevant each token in a sequence is to every other token?
options: Self-attention
Recurrence over hidden states
Dropout between layers
Convolution over token windows
questions.explanation: Self-attention computes relevance scores between all token pairs, which lets transformers capture long-range relationships in parallel. Recurrence processes tokens one at a time.

questions.stem: A team needs a model that predicts next quarter's energy demand as a number. Which type of supervised task is this?
options: Classification
Regression
Clustering
Dimensionality reduction
questions.explanation: Predicting a continuous value is regression. Classification predicts a category; clustering and dimensionality reduction are unsupervised.

questions.stem: Which approach searches for solutions by generating candidates, selecting the fittest and combining or mutating them over generations?
options: Bayesian inference that updates a prior distribution
Gradient descent with backpropagation through layers
Retrieval-augmented generation over a document store
Evolutionary computation, such as genetic algorithms
questions.explanation: Evolutionary computation mimics natural selection: populations of candidate solutions are evaluated, selected, recombined and mutated. It doesn't need gradients.

questions.stem: Why are GPUs, rather than general-purpose CPUs, typically used to train deep learning models?
options: They store far more data on their own local disks than CPUs can
They perform the large parallel matrix operations of training far faster
They encrypt model weights in hardware by default during training
They remove the need for training data to be labeled in advance
questions.explanation: Training is dominated by matrix multiplications that parallelize well. GPUs and TPUs have thousands of cores and high memory bandwidth suited to that work.

questions.stem: What is an embedding in a generative AI system?
options: A numeric vector that represents the meaning of text or other content
A watermark hidden in generated text to identify its source
A compressed copy of the model's weights stored with each prompt
A system prompt that is permanently attached to the model
questions.explanation: Embeddings map content to vectors so that similar meanings sit close together. Vector databases search them to find relevant passages for retrieval.

references.chapterTitle: Fundamentals and Introduction to Large Language Models

questions.stem: A long chat session starts producing answers that ignore instructions given at the very start. What is the most likely technical cause?
options: The embedding model has drifted away from the generator
The model's weights have been updated during the conversation
Early content has fallen outside the model's context window
The vector database has been poisoned by the user's messages
questions.explanation: A model only sees what fits in its context window, measured in tokens. When a conversation grows too long, the earliest content is truncated or summarized away.

questions.stem: Two agents from different vendors need to delegate tasks to each other and exchange results. What does an agent-to-agent (A2A) integration add to the attack surface?
options: Only added network latency, since agents can't pass instructions to each other through task results
Only added cost, because each delegated task consumes tokens from both vendors' quotas and billing plans
Each agent's messages are untrusted input to the other, so check identity and authorization at every hop
Nothing new, because both agents already run inside the same trust boundary by design and share credentials
questions.explanation: Agent-to-agent communication lets one agent's output steer another, so a compromised or manipulated agent can pass along injected instructions. Each hop needs authentication, authorization and output validation.

references.chapterTitle: OWASP AIVSS Core Agentic AI Security Risks

questions.stem: The same prompt sent twice to an LLM returns two differently worded answers. No configuration changed. What explains this?
options: Non-deterministic sampling during generation
Data poisoning in the training set
Model drift between the two requests
A prompt injection hidden in the first answer
questions.explanation: LLMs sample from a probability distribution over next tokens. With temperature above zero, repeated prompts can produce different outputs.

references.chapterTitle: Do Language Models Dream of Electric Sheep?

questions.stem: Which metric balances precision and recall into a single score?
options: Accuracy
Mean squared error
Specificity
F1 score
questions.explanation: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. Accuracy can look high on imbalanced data even when the minority class is missed.

questions.stem: A vendor's model tops a public benchmark, but performs poorly on the company's own support tickets. What is the best next step?
options: Accept the benchmark score, since public benchmarks are standardized
Evaluate it on a representative, held-out sample of the company's own data
Lower the temperature until the support answers become consistent
Fine-tune it on the public benchmark to improve its reliability
questions.explanation: Benchmarks may not reflect a specific domain, and models can be tuned to them. Task-specific evaluation on representative data is the reliable test.

questions.stem: A loan pre-screening model is accurate, but its recommendations affect people's access to credit. How should its outputs be used?
options: With human review of adverse decisions before they take effect
With fully automated execution, since accuracy is high
With outputs hidden from staff, to avoid introducing human bias
With random sampling of approvals only, to save reviewer time
questions.explanation: High-impact decisions about individuals call for human oversight regardless of accuracy. Reviewing adverse outcomes catches errors where the harm is greatest.

questions.stem: Which kind of data is hardest to classify and filter for sensitive content before training?
options: Lookup tables of product codes and their descriptions
Structured data in a database with a defined schema
Numeric sensor readings stored in fixed-width columns
Unstructured data such as documents, chat logs and images
questions.explanation: Unstructured data has no fixed fields, so sensitive content can appear anywhere. Structured data can be classified by column.

questions.stem: A labeling vendor's annotations disagree with each other on 30% of samples. Which data quality dimension is most affected?
options: Completeness of the records
Volume and variety of the dataset
Accuracy and consistency of labels
Timeliness of the labeled data
questions.explanation: High disagreement means labels are unreliable, which directly affects what the model learns. Agreement checks and adjudication improve label quality.

questions.stem: A team replaces names in a dataset with random tokens but keeps a lookup table that maps tokens back to names. How should the result be treated?
options: As synthetic data, because the original values have been replaced
As personal data, because it can be re-identified using the lookup table
As anonymous data, because the names are no longer visible in the records
As public data, because tokens can't be linked to individuals by outsiders
questions.explanation: Tokenization and pseudonymization are reversible when a mapping exists. Under GDPR, pseudonymized data remains personal data.

questions.stem: What is the main privacy appeal of synthetic data for model development?
options: It can never leak information about the real records used to create it
It reproduces statistical patterns without containing real individuals' records
It removes the need to validate model performance against real-world data
It is always more accurate than the real data it was generated from
questions.explanation: Synthetic data can preserve useful patterns without real records. It isn't risk-free: generators can memorize and leak training data, so privacy still needs testing.

questions.stem: An auditor asks where a training dataset came from and what was done to it before training. What answers this?
options: The model card's intended-use section
The model's accuracy report
The data center's access logs
Data provenance and lineage records
questions.explanation: Provenance records origin, and lineage records transformations. Together they let you show where data came from and how it changed.

questions.stem: Records are copied from a CRM, cleaned, labeled and split into training and test sets. At which stage would a tampered record most likely go unnoticed?
options: Any stage without integrity checks, since changes flow straight into the model
No stage, because model training automatically rejects altered records
Only at the test split, because training data is never reviewed by people
Only at acquisition, because later stages always re-validate source records
questions.explanation: Each lifecycle stage is a chance to alter data. Without hashing or validation between stages, a change made anywhere passes through to training.

questions.stem: Attackers add small, carefully crafted changes to malware so a deployed ML detector labels it benign. The detector itself was never modified. What attack is this?
options: A membership inference attack
A data poisoning attack at training time
An evasion attack at inference time
A model extraction attack
questions.explanation: Evasion manipulates inputs to a deployed model to cause misclassification. Poisoning alters training data; extraction copies the model.

questions.stem: Researchers query a face recognition model and reconstruct recognizable images of people in its training set. What attack is this?
options: Backdoor poisoning
Evasion
Model extraction
Model inversion
questions.explanation: Model inversion recovers information about training data from a model's outputs. Extraction aims to copy the model's behavior instead.

references.chapterTitle: Diving Deep: Profiles of the Top 10 LLM Security Risks
references.section: Sensitive data exposure – training data leakage and model inversion

questions.stem: Under a Zero Trust approach to an LLM application, how should the model's own output be treated before it is passed to a database query?
options: As untrusted input that must be validated and parameterized
As trusted if the model is hosted by an approved vendor
As trusted, because it was generated inside the security boundary
As untrusted only when the user is not authenticated
questions.explanation: Model output can carry injected or malformed content. OWASP lists improper output handling (LLM05:2025) because passing it unchecked to databases or shells enables injection attacks.

questions.stem: Which OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025) risk covers attackers manipulating data in a RAG system's vector store or embeddings?
options: LLM10: Unbounded Consumption
LLM02: Sensitive Information Disclosure
LLM08: Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
LLM07: System Prompt Leakage
questions.explanation: The 2025 list added LLM08, Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, covering risks such as poisoned or unauthorized access to embeddings in RAG systems.

questions.stem: An attacker queries a model with specific records to work out whether each record was in its training set. What attack is this?
options: Prompt injection
Membership inference
Evasion
Model inversion
questions.explanation: Membership inference determines whether a given record was used in training, which can itself reveal sensitive facts, such as a patient being in a disease dataset.

questions.stem: Which guardrail checks a chatbot's response for hate speech before the user sees it?
options: Output toxicity classification
Prompt template version control
Model weight signing at load time
Input rate limiting per user
questions.explanation: Output guardrails inspect generated content, for example with a toxicity classifier, and block or rewrite unsafe responses. Rate limiting and signing address other risks.

questions.stem: Which control best protects a model training environment from being reached from the corporate user network?
options: A larger GPU cluster with dedicated capacity
More frequent retraining of the production model
Network segmentation that isolates the AI environment
A stronger password policy for data scientists
questions.explanation: Isolating AI environments limits who and what can reach training data and model artifacts, containing compromises elsewhere on the network.

questions.stem: What does model verification aim to confirm before deployment?
options: That the model was trained on the most recent public internet data available
That the model meets its specified performance, safety and integrity requirements
That the model has the largest parameter count the vendor currently offers
That the model's outputs are identical every time the same prompt is repeated
questions.explanation: Verification checks a model against requirements: evaluation results, safety testing and artifact integrity, such as signatures. Size and recency aren't requirements by themselves.

questions.stem: A user can see why a credit model flagged their application through a list of the top contributing factors. Which responsible AI principle does this support?
options: Availability
Data minimization
Non-repudiation
Explainability
questions.explanation: Giving people understandable reasons for a decision is explainability, which supports transparency and the ability to contest outcomes.

references.chapterTitle: Bias, Explainability, Privacy, and Adversarial Attacks

questions.stem: An input guardrail blocks prompts containing known jailbreak phrases. Why isn't this enough on its own?
options: Input guardrails only work on models that have been fine-tuned in-house by the security team
Attackers can rephrase, so layered controls such as output checks and least privilege are still needed
Blocking phrases always violates the transparency principle, so regulators prohibit the practice
Input guardrails slow responses so much that most users stop using the application
questions.explanation: Pattern-based blocking is easy to bypass with paraphrasing, encoding or multi-turn attacks. Defense in depth combines input checks, output validation and limits on what the model can do.

questions.stem: A company says its chatbot is safe because the system prompt tells it never to reveal internal data. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The approach is sufficient when it's combined with a low temperature and a short context window
The approach is sufficient if the model has also been fine-tuned to obey its system prompt
Instructions can be overridden, so internal data should be kept out of reach or filtered outside the model
The approach is sufficient as long as the system prompt itself is kept confidential from users
questions.explanation: System prompts guide behavior but are not security boundaries; prompt injection and leakage can defeat them. OWASP lists system prompt leakage (LLM07:2025) and advises against relying on prompts for security.

questions.stem: Developers adopt an AI coding assistant. Which risk should the security team address first?
options: The assistant suggesting code in a different style from the team's existing conventions
Developers adopting the tool faster than the security team can publish usage guidance for it
The assistant's monthly license cost growing faster than the team's approved tooling budget
Generated code with vulnerabilities or license issues entering production without review
questions.explanation: AI-generated code can contain insecure patterns or snippets with license obligations. It should pass the same review, testing and scanning as human-written code.

questions.stem: A hospital wants to use an LLM to draft discharge summaries from patient records. Which concern is most specific to this use case?
options: Protected health information exposure and errors in clinical content
Clinicians preferring the summary format used before the tool was introduced
Higher token costs from summarizing long patient records with many notes
Slower response times when many discharge summaries are requested at once
questions.explanation: Healthcare use involves PHI and high-stakes content, so privacy controls (such as HIPAA safeguards and agreements with vendors) and clinician review are essential.

questions.stem: A bank uses ML to approve or decline credit applications. Which requirement is most characteristic of this financial use case?
options: GPU capacity sufficient for training very large language models in-house
Support for multiple languages in the customer-facing application chat
Fairness testing and explainable reasons for adverse decisions
Real-time image generation for personalized credit card marketing campaigns
questions.explanation: Credit decisions affect individuals and are regulated, so lenders must manage bias and be able to explain declines.

questions.stem: A vulnerability team uses an ML model to rank thousands of findings. What is the main benefit?
options: Prioritizing remediation by predicted exploitability and business impact
Eliminating the need to patch lower-ranked vulnerabilities at all
Replacing the asset inventory used to locate affected systems
Guaranteeing that no exploited vulnerability is ever missed
questions.explanation: ML can help focus effort on what is most likely to be exploited and most damaging. It assists prioritization; it doesn't remove the need to patch or guarantee completeness.

questions.stem: An insurer in the EU wants to use AI to assess risk and set prices for individual life and health insurance policies. How is this use generally classified under the EU AI Act?
options: Limited risk, with transparency duties only
Prohibited under Article 5
Minimal risk, with no specific obligations
High-risk, listed in Annex III
questions.explanation: Annex III lists AI systems used for risk assessment and pricing of natural persons in life and health insurance as high-risk, because they affect access to essential services. That brings obligations such as risk management, data governance and human oversight.

references.section: Key Regulations Impacting AI Development and Use

questions.stem: A SOC uses an LLM to summarize alerts and suggest likely causes. What should analysts treat the summaries as?
options: Replacements for the original logs, which can be discarded
Decision support to verify against the underlying evidence
Evidence suitable for legal proceedings without review
Final determinations that close the alert automatically
questions.explanation: AI summaries speed triage but can be wrong. Analysts should verify against source data, and original logs must be kept as evidence.

questions.stem: In the NIST AI RMF, a team documents an AI system's intended purpose, context of use, stakeholders and potential impacts before building it. Which function is this?
options: Govern
Map
Manage
Measure
questions.explanation: Map establishes context: purpose, users, settings and potential impacts, so risks can be identified. Measure analyzes and tracks them; Manage prioritizes and acts on them.

questions.stem: A company fine-tunes a third-party general-purpose model and sells the result under its own brand for use in hiring. What role does the EU AI Act most likely assign the company?
options: Distributor, since it resells another firm's model
Importer, since the base model came from elsewhere
Provider of a high-risk AI system
Deployer only, since it didn't build the base model
questions.explanation: A company that places an AI system on the market under its own name is its provider. Hiring is a high-risk use, so provider obligations such as conformity assessment apply. The Act also says that deployers who rebrand or substantially modify a high-risk system take on provider duties.

references.section: Key Regulations Impacting AI Development and Use

questions.stem: Under the GDPR, what right do people generally have regarding decisions based solely on automated processing that significantly affect them?
options: To receive a full copy of the model's weights and training data on request
To demand that the organization stop using AI for any purpose involving their data
To be paid compensation by the organization whenever an automated decision is made
Not to be subject to them, with exceptions and safeguards such as human intervention
questions.explanation: Article 22 restricts solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects. Where exceptions apply, safeguards include the right to human intervention, to express a view and to contest the decision.

references.chapterTitle: Navigating the Cultural, Social, and Legal Landscapes
references.section: The Case of Data Privacy and Protection in Personalized AI Systems

questions.stem: Which document type sets mandatory, specific requirements that support a high-level AI policy, such as approved model sources and minimum evaluation criteria?
options: A standard
A press release
A mission statement
A guideline
questions.explanation: Policies state intent and direction; standards set mandatory specifics; procedures give step-by-step instructions; guidelines are recommended practice.

questions.stem: Leadership wants one executive accountable for AI strategy, value and risk across all business units. Which role fits?
options: Data protection officer
Network operations manager
Chief financial officer
Chief AI Officer
questions.explanation: A Chief AI Officer coordinates AI strategy, governance and risk enterprise-wide. A DPO has a narrower, privacy-specific mandate that should stay independent.

questions.stem: Which NIST publication applies the AI RMF specifically to generative AI and describes risks such as confabulation?
options: NIST SP 800-53, security and privacy controls
NIST AI 600-1, the Generative AI Profile
NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0
NIST SP 800-61, incident handling guide
questions.explanation: NIST AI 600-1 is a profile of the AI RMF for generative AI. It describes GenAI-specific risks, including confabulation (NIST's term for hallucination), and suggested actions.

questions.stem: An organization runs AI pilots in five departments, each with its own approval process. What is the most effective governance improvement?
options: A ban on new pilots until every department agrees on tools
Five separate policies tailored to each department's preferences
A central intake and inventory with one risk-based approval process
Letting each vendor certify its own product as compliant
questions.explanation: Centralized intake gives visibility and consistent, risk-proportionate decisions. Fragmented approvals create gaps and duplicated effort.

questions.stem: What is the maximum fine under the EU AI Act for using a prohibited AI practice?
options: Up to €35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher
A fixed €1 million per violation, regardless of company size
Up to €10 million or 2% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher
Up to €20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher
questions.explanation: Prohibited practices carry the Act's highest penalty tier: up to €35 million or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover. The 4% figure is the GDPR's upper tier.

references.section: Key Regulations Impacting AI Development and Use

questions.stem: A hiring tool selects women at 60% of the rate it selects men. Under the US EEOC's four-fifths guideline, what does this suggest?
options: Adverse impact only if the tool's overall accuracy is below 80%
No issue, because the tool selects some women
No issue, because the guideline applies only to human recruiters
Possible adverse impact, because 60% is below the 80% threshold
questions.explanation: The four-fifths rule of thumb flags possible adverse impact when one group's selection rate is below 80% of the highest group's rate. It prompts investigation; it isn't a final legal finding.

questions.stem: Which fairness criterion requires that qualified applicants from each group are approved at equal rates?
options: Demographic parity (equal approval rates overall)
Equal opportunity (equal true positive rates)
Individual fairness (similar people treated alike)
Calibration (equal precision of scores)
questions.explanation: Equal opportunity compares true positive rates: among people who truly qualify, each group should be approved equally often. Demographic parity compares overall approval rates regardless of qualification.

references.chapterTitle: Bias, Explainability, Privacy, and Adversarial Attacks

questions.stem: A speech assistant performs much worse for users with certain accents. Which responsible AI principle is most directly at stake?
options: Non-repudiation
Data sovereignty
Inclusiveness
Availability
questions.explanation: Inclusiveness means systems work well for the full range of people who use them. Gaps for accents, languages or disabilities are inclusiveness failures, usually rooted in unrepresentative data.

questions.stem: A model's training data comes mostly from one region, and it performs poorly elsewhere. What type of bias is this?
options: Sampling or representation bias
Automation bias of users
Confirmation bias of reviewers
Recency bias in evaluation
questions.explanation: When training data doesn't represent the population the model serves, performance suffers for underrepresented groups. The fix is better data coverage and evaluation by group.

questions.stem: Employees approve an AI tool's recommendations almost every time, even when they're clearly wrong. What risk is this?
options: Data poisoning
Automation bias
Excessive agency
Model drift
questions.explanation: Automation bias is the tendency to over-trust automated output. It undermines human oversight, so reviewers need training, time and interfaces that encourage real scrutiny.

questions.stem: A team is choosing between two models with similar accuracy. One needs far more energy to train and run. Which consideration does this raise?
options: Explainability of each model's individual predictions
Non-repudiation of outputs from both candidate models
Environmental sustainability of the AI system
Data residency of the two models' training data
questions.explanation: Responsible AI includes environmental impact. When performance is comparable, energy and resource use are legitimate selection criteria.

questions.stem: What is the difference between transparency and explainability?
options: Transparency is openness about how a system is used and governed; explainability is why it gave a specific output
Transparency applies only to open-source models; explainability applies only to closed, proprietary models
Transparency is a legal requirement only; explainability is an engineering practice with no legal standing
They are the same principle, described under two different names in the NIST and ISO frameworks
questions.explanation: Transparency means disclosing that AI is used and how it works and is governed. Explainability means giving understandable reasons for specific outputs. NIST lists them as related but distinct characteristics.

references.chapterTitle: Bias, Explainability, Privacy, and Adversarial Attacks

questions.stem: Fixing a model to equalize false positive rates across groups lowers overall accuracy slightly. How should the team decide?
options: Let the model choose its own fairness metric during training
Always equalize every fairness metric, whatever the effect on accuracy
Always maximize accuracy, because fairness metrics are optional
Weigh the trade-off in context with stakeholders and document the rationale
questions.explanation: Fairness metrics can conflict with each other and with accuracy. The right choice depends on context and harm, and the decision should be made with stakeholders and documented.

references.chapterTitle: Bias, Explainability, Privacy, and Adversarial Attacks

questions.stem: A generative tool can easily produce realistic fake videos of real people. Which societal risk is most relevant?
options: Higher GPU costs from rendering long, high-resolution video
Misinformation and impersonation through deepfakes
Copyright claims over the tool's own interface design
Lower model accuracy when generating short video clips
questions.explanation: Synthetic media can be used to deceive, defraud or defame. Safeguards include content provenance, labeling and usage policies.

references.section: Key Regulations Impacting AI Development and Use

questions.stem: An AI system was developed responsibly, but no one is named as answerable for its outcomes. Which principle is missing?
options: Inclusiveness
Privacy
Accountability
Reliability
questions.explanation: Accountability means specific people or roles are answerable for an AI system's outcomes and have authority to act. Without it, issues go unaddressed.

questions.stem: What is the difference between inherent risk and residual risk?
options: Inherent risk is temporary; residual risk is permanent and can't change
Inherent risk is caused by insiders; residual risk is caused by outside attackers
Inherent risk is technical; residual risk is legal and regulatory
Inherent risk is before controls are applied; residual risk is what remains after them
questions.explanation: Inherent risk is the exposure with no controls. Residual risk remains after controls and must be within the organization's risk appetite or be treated further.

references.chapterTitle: Creating Trustworthy AI: A Lifecycle Risk Management Framework

questions.stem: Which change most increases the blast radius of an AI assistant?
options: Letting it send emails and payments on users' behalf
Moving it to a larger model with a longer context window and more parameters
Letting it search the company intranet to answer questions more completely
Adding a thumbs-up and thumbs-down feedback button under each response
questions.explanation: Blast radius grows with the actions a system can take and the systems it touches. Autonomy over email and payments means a failure or compromise can cause direct harm.

questions.stem: Before launching an AI system that will screen benefit applications, which assessment should the team complete?
options: A cost comparison of the cloud GPU providers that could host it
A penetration test of the office Wi-Fi network used by caseworkers
An AI impact assessment covering effects on individuals and groups
A usability study of the application form that applicants fill in
questions.explanation: Systems that affect people's access to services need an impact assessment covering rights, fairness, safety and privacy. ISO/IEC 42001 also requires AI system impact assessments.

references.chapterTitle: Designing a Well-Governed AI Lifecycle Model

questions.stem: Which approach best quantifies an AI risk for leadership?
options: Describe the model architecture and training pipeline in technical detail
Estimate likelihood and business impact, ideally in financial terms
Report the number of open vulnerabilities across all AI systems
List every model hyperparameter and its current production value
questions.explanation: Leaders decide on risk in business terms. Estimating likelihood and impact, for example expected loss, supports comparison and prioritization.

references.chapterTitle: Creating Trustworthy AI: A Lifecycle Risk Management Framework

questions.stem: A risk is rated high, but the business decides not to launch the feature. Which risk treatment is this?
options: Mitigate
Transfer
Accept
Avoid
questions.explanation: Avoiding risk means not doing the activity that creates it. Mitigation reduces it, transfer shifts it (for example through insurance) and acceptance tolerates it.

questions.stem: A company buys cyber insurance that covers losses from AI-related data breaches. Which risk treatment is this?
options: Transfer
Accept
Mitigate
Avoid
questions.explanation: Insurance transfers part of the financial impact to another party. Accountability for the system and its outcomes stays with the company.

questions.stem: A low-risk internal summarizer is later connected to customer records and allowed to email customers. What should happen?
options: Keep the original low-risk tier, since the model itself is unchanged
Re-tier the use case and reassess risk before the change goes live
Reassess only if a customer complains about an email
Remove the email feature after it has run for a month
questions.explanation: New data sources and new autonomous actions are reassessment triggers. Risk tier depends on use and capability, not just the model.

references.chapterTitle: Creating Trustworthy AI: A Lifecycle Risk Management Framework

questions.stem: Where should identified AI risks, their owners, ratings and treatments be tracked?
options: In a risk register
In the source code repository README
In the system prompt
In the model's training logs
questions.explanation: A risk register records each risk with its owner, rating, treatment and status, so risks are tracked and reviewed over time.

questions.stem: Which factor most increases the risk tier of an AI use case?
options: Use of a model hosted in the same cloud region as the application
Use of a popular, widely adopted open-source machine learning framework
Autonomous decisions that affect people's rights or safety
Use of a model trained by a large and well-known AI vendor
questions.explanation: Tiering weighs impact on people and how much the system acts without human review. Hosting region and tooling matter less to inherent risk.

references.chapterTitle: Creating Trustworthy AI: A Lifecycle Risk Management Framework

questions.stem: Under the GDPR, when must a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) be carried out?
options: Only when personal data is transferred to a country outside the European Union
Only after a personal data breach has occurred and been reported to the authority
Only when an organization has more than 250 employees processing personal data
When processing is likely to result in a high risk to individuals' rights and freedoms
questions.explanation: Article 35 requires a DPIA before processing likely to result in high risk, such as large-scale profiling or systematic monitoring. Many AI uses meet that threshold.

references.chapterTitle: Navigating the Cultural, Social, and Legal Landscapes
references.section: The Case of Data Privacy and Protection in Personalized AI Systems

questions.stem: Customer data was collected to process orders. A team now wants to use it to train a marketing model. Which principle must be checked first?
options: Availability
Purpose limitation
Storage encryption
Data accuracy
questions.explanation: Purpose limitation means data collected for one purpose can't be reused for an incompatible purpose without a lawful basis, such as consent.

questions.stem: Which statement about copyright and AI training data is most accurate?
options: Whether training on copyrighted works is lawful is unsettled and varies by jurisdiction
Training on copyrighted works without a license is banned in every major jurisdiction
Training on any copyrighted work is allowed as fair use in every jurisdiction worldwide
Copyright stops applying to a work once it has been converted into embeddings or weights
questions.explanation: Courts and lawmakers are still deciding how copyright applies to training, and rules differ between countries. Organizations should get legal review and track data sources and licenses.

references.chapterTitle: Navigating the Cultural, Social, and Legal Landscapes
references.section: The Case of Copyright and Intellectual Property in the Age of LLMs

questions.stem: A retention policy says chat transcripts are deleted after 90 days. What must the AI team ensure?
options: Only the copy held in the chat application itself needs to be deleted on schedule
Retention applies only to the transcripts that contain payment card or bank data
Transcripts may be kept beyond 90 days whenever they're useful for model training
Copies in training sets, logs and backups follow the same retention rule
questions.explanation: Retention rules apply to every copy, including those in training data, logs and backups. Otherwise data outlives its permitted period.

questions.stem: Staff paste a client's confidential product designs into a public AI tool. What is the main IP risk?
options: The client's trademarks become invalid automatically
The designs become public domain under copyright law
Loss of trade secret protection and confidentiality
The AI tool receives a patent on the designs
questions.explanation: Trade secrets depend on reasonable steps to keep information confidential. Disclosing them to a third-party service, especially one that may retain or train on inputs, can undermine protection and breach contracts.

questions.stem: A model is trained on data that includes children's personal data collected without parental consent. What is the main concern?
options: The only issue is the cost of storing and labeling the extra data that was collected
The model will be more accurate for younger users, which offsets the consent issue
Children's data is exempt from privacy law when it's used only for model training
The data was unlawfully collected, which can taint the model and require remediation
questions.explanation: Unlawfully collected data creates obligations that extend to models trained on it. Regulators have required deletion of data and, in some cases, of models built from it.

questions.stem: Which type of data is most directly protected by HIPAA in the United States?
options: Export-controlled technical data shared with foreign nationals or companies
Protected health information held by covered entities and their business associates
Payment card data processed and stored by merchants and their processors
All personal data collected by any company operating in the United States
questions.explanation: HIPAA protects health information held by covered entities, such as providers and insurers, and their business associates. Cardholder data falls under PCI DSS.

questions.stem: A team plans to train on data scraped from websites whose terms prohibit automated collection. What is the main risk?
options: Breach of contract or terms of service, in addition to copyright and privacy issues
Only a cost risk, because storing and cleaning scraped data is expensive
No legal risk, because the pages are publicly visible without logging in
Only a performance risk, because scraped web data is noisy and inconsistent
questions.explanation: Publicly visible doesn't mean free to use. Website terms, copyright and privacy law can all restrict scraping and training.

references.chapterTitle: Navigating the Cultural, Social, and Legal Landscapes
references.section: The Case of Copyright and Intellectual Property in the Age of LLMs

questions.stem: A dataset of financial transactions is anonymized, but researchers re-identify people by combining it with public records. What does this show?
options: Financial data can't be linked to individuals
Public records never contain personal information
Anonymization must be tested against linkage with outside data
Anonymized data can always be shared without restriction
questions.explanation: Re-identification through linkage is a well-known risk. Anonymization should be assessed against realistic outside data, and techniques like k-anonymity or differential privacy chosen accordingly.

questions.stem: A vendor's terms allow it to use customer prompts to improve its models. What should a company handling confidential data do?
options: Ask employees to remove customer names from prompts and then proceed with the tool
Accept the terms, since model improvements benefit every customer of the service
Use the tool only in departments that don't usually handle confidential data
Opt out or negotiate terms that prohibit training on its data before use
questions.explanation: Data use terms decide whether confidential inputs can end up in a vendor's models. They should be settled contractually before sensitive data is sent.

questions.stem: Which evidence is most useful when assessing a model vendor's security controls?
options: The vendor's security whitepaper describing its controls and its security culture
A list of the vendor's largest customers and how long each has used the product
A recent independent audit report, such as SOC 2 Type II or ISO/IEC 27001 certification
The vendor's own completed security questionnaire, without supporting evidence
questions.explanation: Independent audits give evidence of controls operating over time. A SOC 2 Type II report covers a period of operation; Type I covers design at a point in time.

questions.stem: An AI vendor uses another company to host its models. What is this other company to you?
options: A fourth party whose risk you inherit through your vendor
A competitor with no relevance to your risk assessment
An internal business unit
Your direct supplier, bound by your contract
questions.explanation: Your vendor's suppliers are fourth parties. Due diligence should ask which subprocessors handle your data and how they are managed.

questions.stem: Which contract clause best protects a company when it stops using an AI service?
options: Priority access to new model features and beta programs
Data return and certified deletion at contract end
A dedicated account manager and quarterly business reviews
A discount for renewing the contract early for three years
questions.explanation: Exit terms should require returning or deleting your data, including copies in logs, backups and any fine-tuned models, and confirming deletion.

questions.stem: Most business units rely on a single foundation model provider. What risk does this create?
options: Lower overall costs from volume discounts negotiated across business units
Better consistency of answers and tone across all business units' applications
A reduced need for each business unit to perform its own vendor due diligence
Concentration risk if that provider fails, changes terms or degrades the model
questions.explanation: Heavy dependence on one provider is concentration risk. Mitigations include contingency plans, abstraction layers and tested alternatives.

questions.stem: Under a shared responsibility model for an IaaS deployment where you run your own model on cloud VMs, who patches the guest operating system?
options: The cloud provider
The customer
No one, since VMs patch themselves
The model's original publisher
questions.explanation: In IaaS, the provider secures the physical and virtualization layers and the customer manages the guest OS, applications and data. Responsibility shifts toward the provider in PaaS and SaaS.

questions.stem: A contract requires the AI vendor to meet stated uptime, response time and security requirements, with remedies if it doesn't. What is this?
options: A service level agreement
A statement of applicability
A memorandum of understanding
A non-disclosure agreement
questions.explanation: SLAs define measurable service commitments and remedies. Security requirements and incident notification can be included in them or in security addenda.

questions.stem: A cloud provider offers confidential computing for model inference. What does this mainly protect against?
options: Loss or interception of data during network transit to the provider
Bias in the model's training data that affects inference results
Exposure of data in use to the host platform and its operators
Prompt injection by end users who submit crafted inference requests
questions.explanation: Confidential computing runs workloads in hardware-based trusted execution environments that protect data while it's processed, including from the host and its administrators.

questions.stem: Before adopting a vendor's AI model, what should due diligence confirm about the model itself?
options: Its provenance, training data sources, license terms and evaluation results
The number of parameters it has, compared with competing vendors' models
Its price per thousand tokens, compared with the market's other offerings
How many other companies already use the model, and in which industries
questions.explanation: Model due diligence covers where it came from, what it was trained on, what you may legally do with it and how it performs and fails.

questions.stem: A vendor refuses any audit rights and won't share security documentation. What should the organization do?
options: Proceed, since many vendors restrict audit rights to protect their confidentiality
Proceed only if the vendor's price is lower than the alternatives that offer audits
Treat this as a risk to escalate, and consider alternative vendors or compensating controls
Ask employees to monitor the vendor's website and news coverage for any incidents
questions.explanation: Without assurance evidence, the vendor's risk can't be assessed. That should be escalated and either mitigated or used to choose another vendor.

questions.stem: Who should have authority to override an AI system's decision in a high-stakes process?
options: Whoever happens to be on shift when the decision appears
Any end user affected by the decision
The model vendor's support team
Named, trained roles defined in governance documents
questions.explanation: Override authority should be assigned to specific roles with the training and context to use it, and documented so it's clear and auditable.

questions.stem: Which record best supports later review of why an AI-assisted decision was made?
options: The total token count and cost for the day the decision was made
A decision log with inputs, outputs, model version and the human reviewer's action
A screenshot of the user interface at the moment the decision was displayed
The model's marketing description and the vendor's published accuracy figures
questions.explanation: Decision logs let auditors reconstruct what the system saw and recommended, which model version was used and what the human did.

questions.stem: A team deploys a model that hasn't passed bias testing, with a manager's approval for an urgent launch. What should be recorded?
options: An exception record with the rationale, approver, compensating controls and expiry date
Only the model's version number and the date it was deployed to production
A note in the team's chat channel explaining why the launch couldn't wait
Nothing formal, since a manager with the authority to accept risk approved the urgent launch
questions.explanation: Exceptions to policy should be formally recorded with who approved them, why, what compensating controls apply and when the exception ends.

questions.stem: Who should audit an AI system's compliance with internal policy?
options: The business unit that requested the system and relies on its output
The data scientists who trained the model and know it best
A function independent of the team that built and runs the system
The vendor that supplied the base model, through its own audit team
questions.explanation: Audits need independence to be credible. Internal audit or an external party should assess systems they didn't build or operate.

questions.stem: Expense reports show several teams paying for AI subscriptions with company cards. What does this reveal?
options: Compliance with the AI acceptable-use policy by teams with budget authority
Shadow AI that bypasses procurement and security review
An efficient procurement process that lets teams move quickly on AI tools
A need to raise card spending limits so teams can buy the tools they need
questions.explanation: Unapproved AI purchases are a common signal of shadow AI. Expense data, along with network and SaaS discovery tools, helps find it.

questions.stem: A model is approved by the same person who built it. Which control is missing?
options: Encryption at rest
Rate limiting
Data minimization
Separation of duties
questions.explanation: Separation of duties means the person who builds a model shouldn't be the one who approves it for production, reducing errors and conflicts of interest.

questions.stem: A customer chatbot answers questions in a human-like way. What disclosure is generally expected under the EU AI Act?
options: Disclosure is needed only for chatbots that sell products or take payments
No disclosure is needed as long as the chatbot's answers are accurate and helpful
Users must be told they are interacting with an AI system, unless it's obvious
Disclosure is needed only if a user directly asks whether they're talking to a person
questions.explanation: Article 50 requires providers to design AI systems that interact with people so users are informed they are dealing with AI, unless that's obvious from the context.

references.section: Key Regulations Impacting AI Development and Use

questions.stem: What distinguishes human-out-of-the-loop operation?
options: The system acts without real-time human approval or monitoring
Humans train and evaluate the model but don't use its outputs directly
A human monitors the system's actions and can intervene at any time
A human approves every action before it takes effect in production systems
questions.explanation: Out-of-the-loop systems act without real-time human involvement, so they suit only lower-risk tasks with strong automated safeguards.

questions.stem: Which EU AI Act obligation requires providers and deployers to ensure their staff have sufficient understanding of AI?
options: Post-market monitoring
AI literacy
Fundamental rights impact assessment
Conformity assessment
questions.explanation: Article 4 requires providers and deployers to take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among staff who deal with AI systems, taking their roles and context into account.

references.section: Key Regulations Impacting AI Development and Use

questions.stem: What should come first when designing an AI security training program?
options: Scheduling one annual all-staff lecture
Purchasing an off-the-shelf course for everyone
Writing an exam for employees to pass
A skills assessment and gap analysis by role
questions.explanation: A gap analysis shows what each role needs to learn, so training targets real needs instead of covering generic material.

questions.stem: Which group most needs training on secure integration of model APIs and handling untrusted model output?
options: Help desk staff who field questions about AI tools
Developers building AI-enabled applications
Business analysts who use AI to draft reports
Procurement staff who buy AI tools from vendors
questions.explanation: Developers decide how prompts, tools and outputs are handled, so they need training on injection, output handling and least privilege.

questions.stem: What should executive AI training focus on?
options: How to configure and secure the GPU clusters that host company models
Hands-on techniques for fine-tuning and evaluating language models
Risk appetite, accountability and the decisions leadership must make
How to write prompts and review outputs for their own daily work
questions.explanation: Executives set risk appetite and approve high-risk uses, so their training should cover governance, accountability and business risk.

questions.stem: Attackers use cloned voices of executives to request urgent wire transfers. Which awareness topic addresses this?
options: Using the approved AI tools to draft payment requests more efficiently
Writing stronger system prompts for the company's internal finance chatbots
Spotting data poisoning in the training sets used by fraud detection models
Recognizing deepfake-enabled social engineering and verifying requests out of band
questions.explanation: Voice and video deepfakes make social engineering more convincing. Training should teach staff to verify unusual requests through a separate, known channel.

questions.stem: Which practice best builds a culture where staff report AI problems early?
options: A blameless reporting channel and visible follow-up on reports
Keeping AI incidents confidential from staff so they don't lose trust in the tools
Penalizing anyone whose prompts cause an incident, so staff are more careful
Reporting only through the vendor's support portal so issues reach the right team
questions.explanation: People report issues when it's safe and they see results. Punitive approaches drive problems underground.

questions.stem: AI tools and threats change quickly. How should AI security training be maintained?
options: Replace it with an annual policy document that every employee must sign
Update it only when an external audit identifies the content as out of date
Update content regularly and provide refreshers when tools or threats change
Deliver it once during onboarding and rely on the written policy afterward
questions.explanation: Training needs regular updates to stay relevant as tools, policies and attack techniques evolve.

questions.stem: What should an AI acceptable-use training module for all staff cover?
options: How to write model cards and risk assessments for production models
Approved tools, what data may be entered and how to report concerns
How the company's AI vendors were selected and what their contracts cover
How transformer models are trained and how attention mechanisms work
questions.explanation: General staff need practical rules: which tools are approved, what data is off-limits and how to raise issues.

questions.stem: After AI security training, the share of employees reporting suspicious AI-generated phishing rises from 10% to 45%. What does this indicate?
options: The training should be discontinued
Phishing attacks have stopped
The training has failed
The training is changing behavior
questions.explanation: Higher reporting rates show staff recognizing and acting on threats, which is the behavior change training aims for.

questions.stem: Which training method best prepares an incident response team for AI-specific incidents?
options: Scenario-based exercises, such as tabletops on prompt injection or model poisoning
Vendor product demonstrations covering each AI tool the company has licensed
Self-paced reading of the EU AI Act and the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications
A lecture series on the history of machine learning and neural network design
questions.explanation: Practicing realistic scenarios builds the judgment and coordination teams need, and exposes gaps in playbooks.

questions.stem: Data scientists know ML well but have little security background. What training is most valuable for them?
options: Presentation and communication skills for explaining models to executives
Company policies on travel, expenses and procurement of cloud resources
Adversarial ML threats, secure data handling and secure MLOps practices
Advanced statistics and new model architectures for their research work
questions.explanation: Data scientists need to understand how models and data are attacked and how to build and handle them securely.

questions.stem: Which role handles day-to-day data quality, metadata and correct use of a training dataset on the owner's behalf?
options: Data steward
Data subject
Data processor
Data owner
questions.explanation: The owner is accountable and sets rules; the steward manages quality, definitions and proper use day to day; the custodian implements technical controls.

questions.stem: Under the GDPR, which party decides the purposes and means of processing personal data used to train a model?
options: The data subject
The controller
The processor
The supervisory authority
questions.explanation: The controller determines why and how personal data is processed. A processor acts on the controller's documented instructions.

references.chapterTitle: Navigating the Cultural, Social, and Legal Landscapes
references.section: The Case of Data Privacy and Protection in Personalized AI Systems

questions.stem: A training dataset is classified as confidential. A team creates embeddings from it for a RAG system. How should the embeddings be classified?
options: As public, because embeddings are numeric vectors rather than readable text
As internal, one level below the source, since embeddings lose some detail
Unclassified until someone requests access, then classified case by case
At least as confidential as the source, since they can reveal its content
questions.explanation: Derived data can leak source content, and embeddings can be partly inverted. Classification should follow data into derived artifacts.

references.chapterTitle: Diving Deep: Profiles of the Top 10 LLM Security Risks
references.section: Sensitive data exposure – training data leakage and model inversion

questions.stem: Several datasets mix real customer records with synthetic records, and no one can tell which is which. What problem does this create?
options: Lineage is lost, so obligations for real personal data can't be applied correctly
Only a storage problem, because duplicate and synthetic files make datasets larger
Only a performance problem, because mixed datasets make training noticeably slower
None, because mixing in synthetic records makes the whole dataset anonymous
questions.explanation: Real and synthetic data carry different obligations and risks. Tagging provenance lets you apply privacy rules and evaluate model quality correctly.

questions.stem: A government customer requires that its data never leaves its country, including for model training and support. What requirement is this?
options: Data minimization and purpose limitation
Data sovereignty and residency
Data portability
Data normalization
questions.explanation: Sovereignty and residency rules restrict where data may be stored, processed and accessed from, including by vendor support staff.

questions.stem: A dataset is handed from a vendor to an internal team and then to a training contractor. What should document each handoff?
options: Email confirmations sent between team leads
A verbal agreement recorded in meeting minutes
The final model's accuracy and evaluation report
Chain of custody records with integrity hashes
questions.explanation: Chain of custody shows who held the data, when and whether it was altered, which supports integrity and accountability.

questions.stem: What should a sensitive data impact assessment for a new training dataset determine?
options: How many records the model needs in order to reach its target accuracy level
Which GPU type and cluster configuration will train fastest on the data
What sensitive data it contains, the risks of using it and the controls required
Which vendor offers the cheapest secure storage for a dataset of this size
questions.explanation: Before use, sensitive datasets should be assessed for the types of sensitive data they hold, the harm misuse could cause and the safeguards needed.

questions.stem: Training data is tagged with labels such as "PII" and "export-controlled" at ingestion. What is the main benefit?
options: Controls and handling rules can be applied automatically downstream
Labels make the data anonymous
Storage costs decrease because tagged data compresses better
The model learns to avoid outputting tagged words
questions.explanation: Classification tags let pipelines enforce access, retention and residency rules consistently as data moves.

questions.stem: Which stage of the AI data lifecycle is most often neglected, leaving sensitive data in old training buckets?
options: Labeling and annotation
Validation before training
Deletion and disposal at end of life
Initial collection and consent capture
questions.explanation: Data is often kept indefinitely after projects end. Lifecycle governance needs retention limits and disposal, including in archives.

questions.stem: A data owner leaves the company, and no one is assigned to their datasets. What risk does this create?
options: Models trained on the data stop working until a new owner is assigned
The datasets become publicly accessible once the owner's account is closed
The cloud provider deletes the datasets after a set period of inactivity
No one approves access, reviews classification or authorizes disposal
questions.explanation: Every dataset needs an accountable owner. Orphaned data drifts out of governance, with stale access and no disposal decisions.

questions.stem: Which practice best supports accountability for how a dataset was used to train models?
options: Renaming datasets after each training run to show which model used them
Logging which model versions consumed each dataset version, and by whom
Compressing and archiving datasets as soon as a training run completes
Storing all datasets in one large bucket so they are easier to locate later
questions.explanation: Linking data versions to model versions and people creates accountability and supports investigations and erasure requests.

questions.stem: A team replaces customer names in log files with consistent placeholders such as "CUSTOMER_1" before analysis. Which technique is this?
options: Homomorphic encryption
k-anonymity generalization
Differential privacy noise added to each record
Pseudonymization through masking
questions.explanation: Replacing identifiers with consistent placeholders is pseudonymization. Records for the same person can still be linked, so it reduces but doesn't remove privacy risk.

questions.stem: In differential privacy, what happens as the privacy budget epsilon gets smaller?
options: Privacy gets weaker, and results get more accurate
Privacy gets stronger, and results get noisier
Privacy is unchanged, but training runs faster
Privacy gets stronger, and results get more accurate
questions.explanation: Smaller epsilon means more noise and a tighter bound on what can be learned about any one person, usually at some cost to accuracy.

questions.stem: Which design choice best reflects Privacy by Design for a new AI feature?
options: Building in minimization and privacy controls from the first design review
Encrypting the feature's data only once a breach or audit makes it necessary
Adding a detailed privacy notice to the feature after it has launched
Waiting for a regulator's or customer's request before reviewing privacy
questions.explanation: Privacy by Design means privacy is considered from the start, with defaults that protect data, rather than added later.

questions.stem: A healthcare provider wants to send patient notes to a cloud LLM service. What must be in place under HIPAA?
options: Nothing, as long as each note is under 1,000 words and names are removed
A SOC 2 Type I report from the provider, with no further agreement needed
A business associate agreement with the service provider
Separate written patient consent for every prompt that includes their notes
questions.explanation: Vendors that handle PHI on a covered entity's behalf are business associates and must sign a BAA, alongside appropriate safeguards.

questions.stem: Which lawful basis is most appropriate for using personal data to train a model for a purpose customers didn't expect?
options: Explicit consent, or another basis supported by a documented legal assessment
Legitimate interest, which applies automatically to training AI on customer data
Implied consent, since customers accepted the terms when they opened an account
No lawful basis is needed as long as the data stays inside the organization
questions.explanation: Unexpected new purposes need a lawful basis. Consent is common; legitimate interest requires a documented balancing test and doesn't apply automatically.

references.chapterTitle: Navigating the Cultural, Social, and Legal Landscapes
references.section: The Case of Data Privacy and Protection in Personalized AI Systems

questions.stem: A model trained without demographic data still produces biased outcomes because it learned from historical decisions. What does this show about privacy controls?
options: Bias can only occur when demographic data is present in the training set
Historical decision data is always neutral, so the model must be misconfigured
Privacy controls such as minimization always eliminate bias from model outputs
Removing sensitive attributes doesn't prevent bias; fairness needs its own testing
questions.explanation: Minimizing sensitive data protects privacy but can hide bias from view. Fairness needs its own testing, sometimes using protected attributes under strict controls.

references.chapterTitle: Navigating the Cultural, Social, and Legal Landscapes
references.section: The Case of Algorithmic Bias and Discrimination in AI-Powered Decision Making

questions.stem: Which technique adds random noise to individual data points before they are sent for collection, so the collector never sees the true values?
options: Tokenization
Local differential privacy
Hashing
Central differential privacy
questions.explanation: In local differential privacy, noise is added on the user's device. In central differential privacy, a trusted curator holds the real data and adds noise to results.

questions.stem: An AI support tool will process data of California residents. Which law is most directly relevant to their privacy rights?
options: The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act's privacy rule
The EU General Data Protection Regulation, since it covers all personal data worldwide
The California Consumer Privacy Act, as amended by the CPRA
The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act
questions.explanation: The CCPA, amended by the CPRA, gives California residents rights over their personal information, including to know, delete and opt out of sale or sharing.

questions.stem: Masking hides data in a test environment, but developers can still query the original production database. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, because the masked test copy already protects the data from developers
Masking should be replaced with longer passwords on the test environment accounts
Developers should mask production data themselves before using it in their tests
The masking control is bypassed, so access to production data must also be restricted
questions.explanation: A privacy control only works if it can't be routed around. Access to the unmasked source must be limited too.

questions.stem: An attacker adds training images that look correctly labeled to a human reviewer, yet cause targeted misclassification later. What is this?
options: A model extraction attack
A clean-label poisoning attack
A label-flipping attack
An evasion attack at inference
questions.explanation: Clean-label poisoning uses samples whose labels look correct, so manual review doesn't catch them. Label flipping changes labels visibly.

questions.stem: Which control best detects poisoned samples before training?
options: Raising the learning rate so training finishes before attackers can add samples
Removing the validation set so more of the clean data is available for training
Statistical outlier and anomaly detection on incoming data, with provenance checks
Training for more epochs so the poisoned samples are averaged out by clean data
questions.explanation: Screening data for anomalies and confirming its source catches many poisoned samples before they shape the model.

questions.stem: A training set includes thousands of web pages from a domain the attacker recently bought. What poisoning technique is this?
options: Poisoning through control of a web source that gets scraped
Membership inference through pages the crawler indexed
Evasion through adversarial images placed on the web pages
Model inversion through content collected by the crawler
questions.explanation: Attackers can buy expired domains or edit pages they know will be crawled, seeding training data with malicious content. Source vetting and snapshots with hashes reduce this.

questions.stem: A model repeats a customer's full home address when prompted with part of it. What happened?
options: The model memorized training data and is leaking it
The vector database is running out of space
A prompt injection changed the model's weights
The model is hallucinating an address
questions.explanation: Models can memorize rare or repeated training records and reproduce them. Deduplication, scrubbing personal data and differential privacy reduce this.

references.chapterTitle: Diving Deep: Profiles of the Top 10 LLM Security Risks
references.section: Sensitive data exposure – training data leakage and model inversion

questions.stem: Who should be able to modify an approved training dataset?
options: Any data scientist on the team, since they understand the data best
Only authorized roles, through a controlled and logged change process
The training pipeline itself, which can relabel records it judges incorrect
Anyone with read access to the bucket, since changes are usually small
questions.explanation: Restricting and logging write access protects dataset integrity and makes unauthorized changes detectable.

questions.stem: A fine-tuning dataset downloaded from a public hub contains hidden trigger phrases. What should have caught this?
options: Increasing the batch size during the fine-tuning run
Training on a larger GPU cluster with more memory
Vetting and scanning third-party datasets before use
Lowering the model's temperature after fine-tuning
questions.explanation: Public datasets should be treated as untrusted: check provenance, scan content and test the resulting model for unexpected behavior.

questions.stem: Why is user feedback that automatically flows into retraining a poisoning risk?
options: Feedback always contains customers' personal data, which can't be used for training
Feedback makes each retrained model larger, which weakens its resistance to attacks
Feedback can't be stored securely, so it may be altered before retraining begins
Attackers can submit crafted feedback that shifts model behavior
questions.explanation: Online learning from user input lets attackers steer the model. Feedback should be validated, rate-limited and reviewed before training.

questions.stem: How can a team check whether a trained model has a backdoor?
options: Measure its inference latency and compare it with the vendor's published figures
Review its model card and the evaluation results the publisher reported for it
Test it with candidate triggers and look for unusual behavior on specific inputs
Check its overall accuracy on the standard held-out test set used during training
questions.explanation: Backdoored models usually perform normally on standard tests. Targeted testing and trigger-detection methods are needed to find them.

references.chapterTitle: Model Tampering with Trojan Horses and Model Reprogramming

questions.stem: A company wants to use generated synthetic data to augment training. What should it confirm first?
options: That the synthetic data uses the same file format and schema as the real training data
That the synthetic data matches real distributions and doesn't leak real records
That the synthetic data was generated by the same model the team plans to fine-tune
That the synthetic dataset is larger than the real dataset it will be combined with
questions.explanation: Synthetic data should be validated for fidelity and checked for privacy leakage before it is trusted for training.

questions.stem: Which tool continuously finds and classifies sensitive data across cloud storage, including vector databases and training buckets?
options: Data security posture management (DSPM)
A container image registry with scanning
A cloud access security broker (CASB)
A web application firewall (WAF)
questions.explanation: DSPM discovers where sensitive data lives in the cloud, how it's classified and who can access it.

questions.stem: Where should API keys for a model provider be stored?
options: In the model's system prompt, so tools the model calls can use them
In a shared spreadsheet that only the team's members can open
In the application's source code repository, in an encrypted config file
In a secrets manager with access control, rotation and audit logging
questions.explanation: Secrets managers protect credentials, control and log access and support rotation. Keys in code or prompts leak easily.

questions.stem: Why should encryption keys be rotated on a schedule?
options: To make encrypted training data load faster during each training run
To keep encrypted data readable by systems that use older algorithms
To reduce the storage space that the encrypted training data takes up
To limit how much data is exposed if a key is compromised
questions.explanation: Rotation limits the amount of data protected by any one key and the window in which a stolen key is useful.

questions.stem: Which protects data moving between a RAG application and its vector database?
options: Tokenization of each user's name before retrieval
Rate limiting on the vector database's query API
TLS encryption in transit, with certificate validation
Encryption at rest on the vector database's disks
questions.explanation: Data in transit needs TLS. Encryption at rest protects stored data but not traffic between services.

questions.stem: An organization uses bring-your-own-key (BYOK) with a cloud AI service. What does this give it?
options: Exemption from the provider's shared responsibility model for that service
Control over key lifecycle, including the ability to revoke the key to cut off access
Guaranteed protection of data while the provider is processing it in memory on its own servers
Automatic anonymization of all personal data sent to the provider's service
questions.explanation: BYOK lets the customer create, rotate and revoke keys. It doesn't protect data in use; that needs confidential computing or similar.

questions.stem: An agent should only read customer records needed for the ticket it is handling. Which approach enforces this?
options: Purpose-based access that scopes data to the current task
Logging the agent's queries without restricting them
Encrypting the database at rest
Giving the agent read access to the whole customer database
questions.explanation: Purpose-based or task-scoped access limits each request to the data its purpose needs, reducing exposure if the agent is misused.

references.chapterTitle: Designing LLM Systems for Security: Architecture, Controls, and Best Practices

questions.stem: A DLP tool flags a prompt containing source code from a restricted repository being sent to an external AI tool. What should happen?
options: Allow it, but notify the employee's manager by email afterward
Allow it, since source code isn't personal data under privacy law
Block or redact it according to policy, and alert security
Disable the employee's account until HR completes a review
questions.explanation: DLP should enforce policy on sensitive data leaving the organization, including code, and alert so the event can be reviewed.

questions.stem: Who should hold the ability to both manage encryption keys and access the encrypted training data?
options: The model vendor's operations team, under contract
Different people or roles, to separate duties
The same administrator, so access can be granted quickly
All data scientists who train models on the data
questions.explanation: Separating key management from data access means no single person can decrypt data unilaterally.

questions.stem: Which method sanitizes failed hard drives that will not be reused and leave the organization's control?
options: Deleting the partition table and reformatting the drives
Degaussing them and returning them under warranty
A single full overwrite of every sector with zeros
Physical destruction, such as shredding or disintegration
