questions.explanation: Failed drives can't be reliably overwritten or securely erased, because the drive no longer accepts commands. When media won't be reused and is leaving your control, physical destruction is the dependable option under NIST SP 800-88.

questions.stem: Who should be accountable for a production model's performance, risk and retirement?
options: A named model owner
The cloud provider
The end users
The last engineer to deploy it
questions.explanation: Each model needs an accountable owner who approves changes, monitors risk and decides on retirement.

questions.stem: A model's risk classification determines how much review it needs before release. What should drive the classification?
options: The programming language and framework it was built in
Its use case impact, autonomy and data sensitivity
The number of people on the team that maintains it
The size of its weights file and its parameter count
questions.explanation: Risk classification reflects potential harm, which depends on what the model is used for, how independently it acts and what data it handles.

references.chapterTitle: Creating Trustworthy AI: A Lifecycle Risk Management Framework

questions.stem: A new model version underperforms after release. What capability lets the team recover quickly?
options: A tested rollback to the previous approved version
Turning off monitoring alerts until the model stabilizes
Raising the inference timeout so requests don't fail
Retraining a new model from scratch on the latest data
questions.explanation: Keeping prior versions in the registry and testing rollback lets teams restore a known-good model fast.

questions.stem: Which should be monitored to detect that a production model's input data has changed?
options: The model file's checksum, compared with the approved version
Inference latency, compared with the service level agreement
Input feature distributions compared with the training baseline
The number of requests per minute, compared with last month
questions.explanation: Data drift shows up as shifts in input distributions. Monitoring them against a baseline triggers investigation or retraining.

references.chapterTitle: Designing an Enterprise ML Architecture with AWS ML Services

questions.stem: An audit trail must show which data events affected a model without exposing the personal data itself. What approach fits?
options: Log every raw record in full, with access limited to auditors
Log only the model's final accuracy after each data change
Log nothing about data events, to protect people's privacy
Log identifiers, hashes and metadata rather than raw personal data
questions.explanation: Privacy-preserving audit trails record what happened and to which records, through hashes or IDs, without copying sensitive content into logs.

questions.stem: Who should approve promotion of a high-risk model to production?
options: Any senior member of the development team, once the testing results look acceptable to them
Designated approvers under the governance workflow, separate from the developers
The model vendor, if the model is built on the vendor's base model
The developer who trained it, since they know the model best
questions.explanation: Approval workflows assign authority by risk tier and separate building from approving.

references.chapterTitle: Designing a Well-Governed AI Lifecycle Model

questions.stem: Which input control protects a deployed model from malformed or malicious requests?
options: Input validation and sanitization before inference
Increasing the model's context window
Reducing logging to lower response times
Switching to a larger, more capable model that resists bad input
questions.explanation: Validating inputs, such as type, length and format, and filtering known attack patterns reduces exposure to malformed and malicious input.

questions.stem: A model is scheduled for an update to fix a vulnerability. What should the update process include?
options: Immediate deployment to all users, since the fix closes a vulnerability
Deleting the previous version first so it can't be redeployed by mistake
Testing, approval, staged deployment and a rollback plan
Notifying users only after the update is fully deployed and stable
questions.explanation: Controlled updates reduce the chance that a fix introduces new problems, and keep a path back if it does.

questions.stem: What does a model registry provide?
options: A database of the training labels used for each version of each model
A backup of the source code used to train and serve each model
A list of all the users and applications that call each model's endpoint
A system of record for model versions, metadata, approvals and status
questions.explanation: Registries track each model version, its lineage, approvals and deployment status, forming the source of truth for what may run.

questions.stem: A deployed model starts returning unusually confident predictions on inputs very different from training data. What should monitoring flag?
options: A hardware upgrade on the inference servers that changed the outputs
A performance improvement that should be recorded in the model card
An anomaly that may indicate out-of-distribution inputs or an attack
Normal behavior, since confident predictions show the model is working well
questions.explanation: Unusual output patterns can signal distribution shift or adversarial input. Monitoring should flag them for investigation.

references.chapterTitle: Bias, Explainability, Privacy, and Adversarial Attacks

questions.stem: Which control most directly protects the confidentiality of model weights stored in a registry?
options: Strict access control with logging, plus encryption at rest
Publishing the weights' hash so anyone can check them
Increasing the API rate limits for internal users
Moving the registry to servers with more GPU memory
questions.explanation: Weights are valuable IP. Restricting and logging access and encrypting them at rest protect against theft.

questions.stem: A model's weights are altered by an insider. Which control would detect this before serving?
options: User feedback on responses
Signature or hash verification at load time
Output toxicity filtering applied to each response before display
A larger context window
questions.explanation: Verifying signatures or hashes when loading a model detects unauthorized changes.

references.chapterTitle: Source Code, Build, and Deployment Management

questions.stem: Under heavy load, a model API should keep serving basic answers instead of failing outright. What design principle is this?
options: Fail open
Single point of failure
Security through obscurity
Graceful degradation
questions.explanation: Graceful degradation keeps core service available with reduced features under stress, protecting availability.

questions.stem: Which control limits how much one customer can query a model API each month?
options: Encryption at rest
Data masking
Quota enforcement
Model watermarking
questions.explanation: Quotas cap usage per client, protecting availability and cost and making extraction attacks more expensive.

questions.stem: An attacker is building a copy of your model from its outputs. Which combination best reduces this risk?
options: Removing authentication on the API so all traffic can be monitored together
Publishing the model card with full details of its training and architecture
Encrypting the model's weights at rest and in all of its backup copies
Rate limits, monitoring for systematic queries and limiting output detail
questions.explanation: Model extraction relies on many queries and rich outputs. Limiting both, and detecting extraction patterns, raises the cost.

questions.stem: Which practice keeps track of every change to a model's weights and configuration?
options: Caching of model responses with timestamps
Version control for model artifacts
Compression of model files
Load balancing across replicas
questions.explanation: Versioning models and their configuration supports integrity, rollback and auditing.

questions.stem: Watermarking AI-generated text helps with which goal?
options: Detecting that content was produced by a particular model
Encrypting the generated text so only the user can read it
Making the model generate text faster and more cheaply
Preventing anyone from editing or reusing the content
questions.explanation: Output watermarks embed detectable signals in generated content to help identify its source. They can be weakened by editing, so they aren't a complete control.

questions.stem: A proprietary algorithm used in preprocessing is a trade secret. How should it be protected?
options: Embedding it in the system prompt so the model applies it consistently and it stays out of the source code
Publishing it openly to build trust with customers and regulators
Sharing it with all vendors so they can integrate with it correctly
Access restrictions, confidentiality agreements and limited exposure through APIs
questions.explanation: Trade secret protection depends on keeping information confidential with reasonable measures, technical and contractual.

questions.stem: An attacker floods a model API with expensive requests to make it unavailable. Which part of the CIA triad is targeted?
options: Availability
Confidentiality
Integrity
Non-repudiation
questions.explanation: Denial-of-service and resource exhaustion attacks target availability. OWASP calls this unbounded consumption (LLM10:2025).

questions.stem: A team wants to use an open-weight foundation model. Which risk is specific to pre-trained models from outside sources?
options: Incompatibility with the organization's existing HTTPS and TLS configuration
Higher electricity costs for inference compared with smaller in-house models
Hidden backdoors or biases introduced during training you didn't control
Longer code review cycles because the model's source code is very large
questions.explanation: You can't see how an external model was trained, so it may carry backdoors, unsafe behavior or bias. Test and verify before use.

references.chapterTitle: The AI Threat Landscape: Dissecting the Risks and Attack Vectors

questions.stem: How should a team confirm a downloaded dataset hasn't been altered since publication?
options: Compare the file's name and size with the publisher's website listing
Compare its cryptographic hash with the one the publisher provides
Check that the file opens without errors and has the expected columns
Count the rows and confirm the total matches the dataset's description
questions.explanation: Matching a published hash, ideally from a signed source, confirms integrity. Row counts and file names don't detect tampering.

questions.stem: A public dataset includes personal data scraped without consent. What risk does using it create?
options: No risk, because the data was already publicly available online
Privacy violations that can carry into models trained on it
Only an accuracy risk, because scraped personal data is often outdated
Only a storage risk, because personal data must be kept in encrypted form
questions.explanation: Using unlawfully collected data can create legal exposure for the organization and its models.

references.chapterTitle: Navigating the Cultural, Social, and Legal Landscapes

questions.stem: A model vendor can't explain where its training data came from. What should the buyer do?
options: Treat it as a provenance risk and require assurances or choose another vendor
Use the model only for internal tasks, where provenance doesn't matter
Accept it, and ask the vendor to remove any problem data if it is found later
Ignore it, since the training data is the vendor's concern, not the buyer's
questions.explanation: Unknown data provenance hides legal, privacy and quality risks. Buyers should require transparency or contractual assurances.

questions.stem: A model hub shows a model with many downloads and a verified publisher badge. What should a team still do before deploying it?
options: Only check the license to confirm that commercial use is permitted
Only read the model's description and the publisher's usage examples
Scan the files, verify hashes or signatures and test the model's behavior
Nothing more, since many downloads and a verified badge show it's safe
questions.explanation: Popularity and badges reduce some risk but don't prove a model is safe. Scanning, integrity checks and behavioral testing are still needed.

references.chapterTitle: The AI Threat Landscape: Dissecting the Risks and Attack Vectors

questions.stem: A fine-tuned model is built on a base model whose license forbids certain uses. What happens to that restriction?
options: It applies only to the base model's original publisher
It becomes optional after one year
It disappears once the model is fine-tuned
It usually carries over to the derived model
questions.explanation: Many model licenses bind derivatives. Fine-tuning generally doesn't remove the base model's license terms.

questions.stem: Which document should a vendor provide listing the datasets and models used to build its AI product?
options: A marketing datasheet
An AI bill of materials
A privacy notice
A service invoice
questions.explanation: An AIBOM lists AI components, such as models and datasets, with their sources and versions.

questions.stem: A data vendor's dataset is later found to contain poisoned samples. Which practice limits the damage?
options: Tracking which models used each vendor dataset version
Using vendor datasets only for testing, never for training
Storing each vendor dataset in a separate cloud region
Renaming vendor datasets so their origin is easy to see
questions.explanation: Lineage lets you find every affected model quickly and retrain or roll back.

questions.stem: Which contract term helps manage data supply chain risk with a dataset vendor?
options: A clause allowing the vendor to use the buyer's logo in marketing
A fixed delivery date with penalties for late delivery of the data
Warranties about lawful collection and rights to use the data
Free replacement of storage media that arrives damaged in shipping
questions.explanation: Warranties and indemnities about data rights and collection shift legal risk and set expectations for the vendor.

questions.stem: What makes a foundation model a supply chain risk for many organizations at once?
options: It usually can't be fine-tuned by the organizations that use it
It usually runs on only one cloud provider's infrastructure
It usually has less documentation than smaller task-specific models
Many applications depend on it, so one flaw spreads widely
questions.explanation: When many systems build on one foundation model, a vulnerability or bias in it affects all of them.

questions.stem: A team uses an open-source library to load and preprocess training data. What supply chain control applies?
options: Always install the latest version automatically so fixes arrive quickly
Copy the library's code into the project so it doesn't change unexpectedly
Pin versions, scan dependencies for vulnerabilities and verify package integrity
Avoid recording the version used, so upgrades don't need code changes
questions.explanation: Dependencies are part of the AI supply chain. Pinning, scanning and integrity checks reduce the risk of compromised or vulnerable packages.

references.chapterTitle: Source Code, Build, and Deployment Management

questions.stem: An AI application layers input filtering, output validation, least-privilege tools and monitoring. Which design principle is this?
options: Defense in depth
Single sign-on
Fail open
Security through obscurity
questions.explanation: Defense in depth stacks independent controls so one failure doesn't expose the system. No single guardrail is reliable against prompt injection.

references.chapterTitle: Designing LLM Systems for Security: Architecture, Controls, and Best Practices

questions.stem: A new AI feature ships with all tools enabled and logging off until someone requests changes. Which principle does this violate?
options: Non-repudiation
Secure by default
Separation of duties
Data minimization
questions.explanation: Secure defaults mean the shipped configuration is the safe one: least functionality enabled and logging on, with risky features opted into deliberately.

questions.stem: When threat modeling an LLM application, which component is most often missed as a source of untrusted input?
options: The billing database that tracks token usage
The HTTPS certificate on the application
The user's login page and session cookies
Tool and API responses returned to the model
questions.explanation: Responses from tools and APIs re-enter the model's context and can carry injected instructions. They need the same distrust as user input.

questions.stem: A team must choose between a large model with high latency and cost, and a smaller model that meets accuracy needs. What should guide the decision?
options: Choosing whichever model the vendor recommends for this type of use case
Whether the smaller model meets the use case's accuracy, security and latency needs
Always choosing the largest available model, since it will be the most capable
Always choosing the cheapest available model, since costs grow with usage
questions.explanation: Architecture decisions balance requirements. A smaller model that meets them can cut cost, latency and attack surface.

references.chapterTitle: Designing Generative AI Platforms and Solutions

questions.stem: An agent's tools all share one service account with broad rights. What is the best architectural change?
options: Encrypt the service account's password and rotate it yearly
Add a second, identical service account as a backup
Give each tool its own scoped identity and permissions
Move the service account's credentials into the system prompt
questions.explanation: Separate, scoped identities per tool limit what a compromised or misused tool can do and make actions attributable.

references.chapterTitle: Designing LLM Systems for Security: Architecture, Controls, and Best Practices

questions.stem: Which question is most important when deciding whether to build an AI capability in-house or buy it from a vendor?
options: Which option lets you meet your security, data and compliance requirements
Which option uses the programming language your developers know best
Which option your competitors have chosen for similar AI capabilities
Which option the industry analysts ranked highest in their latest report
questions.explanation: Build-versus-buy turns on control, data handling, compliance, skills and cost. Security and data requirements can rule options out.

questions.stem: A RAG system pulls content from the public web at query time. Which architectural safeguard matters most?
options: Use a larger embedding model so retrieval picks the most relevant pages more often
Cache the web pages so they load faster and are consistent across repeated queries
Trust content only from sites that have valid HTTPS certificates and good reputations
Treat web content as untrusted data, kept apart from instructions and privileged tools
questions.explanation: Live web content is attacker-controllable. It must be kept away from instructions and high-privilege actions to limit indirect injection.

references.section: Access to Live External Data Sources

questions.stem: Which architecture pattern routes all model calls through one service that enforces authentication, rate limits, logging and content policy?
options: A direct client-to-model connection
An AI gateway
A flat network
A peer-to-peer mesh
questions.explanation: An AI gateway centralizes enforcement and visibility for model traffic, so policies apply consistently across applications.

references.chapterTitle: Designing LLM Systems for Security: Architecture, Controls, and Best Practices

questions.stem: Which is a key hardening step for a cloud-hosted model endpoint?
options: Use private endpoints and restrict network access to approved clients
Use the cloud account's root credentials so the service never lacks permissions
Disable TLS between internal services to reduce inference latency
Expose the endpoint publicly so testers and partners can reach it more easily
questions.explanation: Private networking, restricted ingress and least-privilege service identities shrink an endpoint's exposure.

questions.stem: Why should training and inference run in separate environments?
options: So that the costs of training and inference appear on separate cloud bills
Because inference and training must be written in different programming languages
Because training never needs network access, while inference always does
So a compromise of one doesn't expose the other's data, models and credentials
questions.explanation: Separating environments limits blast radius. Training holds large datasets and broad access; inference faces users.

questions.stem: A hybrid deployment trains models on-premises and serves them in the cloud. What is a key security concern?
options: Matching the hardware vendors and GPU models used in both environments
Using the same hostnames and IP address ranges in both environments
Securing the transfer and integrity of model artifacts between environments
Keeping the clocks of the two environments synchronized to the same time source
questions.explanation: Artifacts crossing environments need protected transport and integrity checks so they can't be swapped or altered in transit.

questions.stem: Which control prevents a single tenant's batch job from monopolizing a shared inference cluster?
options: Compute throttling and per-tenant resource quotas
Moving every tenant's jobs onto a single shared queue
Disabling monitoring on the cluster to free resources
Giving each tenant administrator rights on the cluster
questions.explanation: Throttling and quotas keep one workload from starving others, protecting availability in shared environments.

questions.stem: What is the main reason to apply secure baseline configurations to AI servers?
options: To reduce GPU costs by allowing servers to run at higher utilization
To improve model accuracy by giving workloads more consistent resources
To make servers boot faster and recover more quickly after updates
To remove unnecessary services and settings that attackers could exploit
questions.explanation: Hardening baselines reduce attack surface and make configurations consistent and auditable.

questions.stem: An AI lab stores model weights on servers in an unlocked room. Which control category is lacking?
options: Prompt filtering
Model monitoring
Physical security
Data labeling
questions.explanation: Physical access to servers can bypass logical controls. Locked, monitored spaces with access control protect AI hardware and data.

questions.stem: Containers running model inference all share the same host kernel. Which control improves isolation?
options: Turning off container image scanning to speed up deployment
Sandboxed runtimes or VM-based isolation for untrusted workloads
Sharing one container across all tenants to reduce overhead
Running all containers as root so permissions are consistent
questions.explanation: Containers share a kernel, so stronger isolation such as sandboxed runtimes or lightweight VMs is used for untrusted or multi-tenant workloads.

questions.stem: A data center's cooling fails while GPU clusters run at full load. Which risk is most immediate?
options: Model extraction while the cluster's monitoring is degraded
Hardware damage and loss of availability from overheating
Prompt injection through the cluster's management interface
Data poisoning of training jobs that were running at the time
questions.explanation: High-density AI hardware generates heat quickly. Cooling and power failures threaten availability and equipment.

questions.stem: Which practice ensures AI infrastructure can be rebuilt consistently and securely after an incident?
options: Detailed configuration notes kept by the engineer who built each system
Restoring settings from full disk images taken when systems were built
Manual configuration by whoever is on call, using the vendor's guides
Infrastructure as code with reviewed, version-controlled templates
questions.explanation: Version-controlled infrastructure as code makes environments reproducible and changes reviewable, supporting recovery and auditing.

questions.stem: Which control ensures a model container deployed to production hasn't been altered after it was built?
options: Signing the image at build time and verifying the signature at deploy time
Scanning the image for vulnerabilities once a year and after major changes
Building the image on a trusted developer laptop and uploading it manually
Tagging the image as "latest" so only the newest build is ever deployed
questions.explanation: Signing and verification create integrity from build to deploy, so unsigned or altered images are rejected.

references.chapterTitle: Source Code, Build, and Deployment Management

questions.stem: A pipeline's service account has write access to every bucket and model registry in the company. What is the risk?
options: Training costs will rise because jobs can read more data than needed
The pipeline will run faster than the review process can keep up with
A compromised pipeline can tamper with data and models everywhere
The pipeline's logs will be too large to review for problems
questions.explanation: Pipelines are prime targets. Their credentials should be scoped to the resources each stage needs.

references.chapterTitle: Source Code, Build, and Deployment Management

questions.stem: Which check should run during data ingestion to catch malformed or unexpected records?
options: Load testing of the ingestion service under peak volume
User acceptance testing of the finished model
Schema and data validation against expected formats and ranges
Model accuracy testing on a held-out test set after each training run
questions.explanation: Validating schema, types and value ranges at ingestion stops corrupted or malicious data before it reaches training.

questions.stem: Why should training and deployment pipelines record every artifact's hash?
options: To prove each artifact's integrity and trace it through the pipeline
To speed up training by caching unchanged artifacts between pipeline runs
To replace access control on the artifact storage
To make each artifact smaller and faster to transfer
questions.explanation: Hashes let you verify artifacts haven't changed and link outputs to inputs, supporting lineage and forensics.

questions.stem: A model passes accuracy tests but fails a new safety evaluation. What should the pipeline gate do?
options: Promote it, since it passed the accuracy tests that the team defined first
Block promotion until the failure is resolved or formally accepted
Remove the new safety test, since it wasn't part of the original requirements
Promote it to half of users and watch the safety metrics in production
questions.explanation: Gates should require all defined checks, including safety and security, before promotion.

references.chapterTitle: Designing an Enterprise ML Architecture with AWS ML Services

questions.stem: Which packaging practice reduces risk when distributing a trained model internally?
options: Removing version information so teams always use the newest copy
Sending the weights to each team by email or through a shared drive
Using whichever serialization format the training framework saves by default
Using a safe serialization format and including a signed manifest
questions.explanation: Safe formats avoid code execution on load, and signed manifests let recipients verify contents.

references.chapterTitle: Model Tampering with Trojan Horses and Model Reprogramming

questions.stem: A team retrains a model nightly from production feedback with no human review. What is the biggest risk?
options: Poisoned or low-quality data reaching production automatically
Training for too few epochs to learn from each night's feedback
Storing too few logs to explain why the model changed overnight
Using too little compute because nightly jobs share resources
questions.explanation: Fully automated retraining from live data gives attackers a path into the model. Add validation, review and gating.

questions.stem: Which practice lets a team reproduce exactly how a production model was trained?
options: Saving the accuracy score and the name of the engineer who trained it
Keeping only the final weights and the date they were produced
Recording the training date and the cloud region where it was trained
Versioning code, data, configuration and environment together
questions.explanation: Reproducibility needs all inputs to training under version control. It supports audits, forensics and rebuilding after incidents.

references.chapterTitle: Designing an Enterprise ML Architecture with AWS ML Services

questions.stem: What is machine unlearning?
options: Lowering a model's learning rate over time so it gradually forgets older patterns
Deleting a model and all of its versions from the registry
Removing the influence of specific training data from a trained model
Training a model on unlabeled data instead of labeled data
questions.explanation: Machine unlearning aims to make a model behave as if certain data had never been used. Exact unlearning often means retraining without that data.

references.chapterTitle: Navigating the Cultural, Social, and Legal Landscapes

questions.stem: Secrets used by the training pipeline appear in plain text in build logs. What should be done?
options: Delete the logs and take no other action, since the exposure was internal
Rotate the exposed secrets and mask secrets in pipeline output
Increase the log retention period so the exposure can be investigated later
Make the logs private and keep the secrets, since only the team saw them
questions.explanation: Exposed secrets must be rotated, since anyone who saw the logs may have them. Pipelines should mask secrets in output.

questions.stem: Which control most directly stops an LLM from returning a user's credit card number in a response?
options: A lower temperature setting for all responses
Output filtering that detects and redacts card numbers
A larger model that follows instructions more reliably
A longer system prompt that forbids sharing card data
questions.explanation: Output guardrails catch sensitive data before it reaches the user, independent of how the model was prompted.

questions.stem: An agent can delete files. What guardrail is most appropriate for this tool?
options: Let the agent delete files freely, but log every deletion
Allow deletion only of files the agent itself created
Allow deletion only outside business hours, when fewer users are affected
Require explicit human confirmation before deletion runs
questions.explanation: High-impact, irreversible actions should require human approval, enforced by the orchestration layer.

questions.stem: What does load testing an LLM application reveal?
options: How it performs and fails under expected and peak traffic
Whether its training data was poisoned before it was deployed
Whether its license allows commercial use at high volume
Whether its outputs are biased against particular groups of users
questions.explanation: Load testing checks capacity and behavior under traffic, including whether guardrails and rate limits still work under stress.

questions.stem: A chatbot crashes when it receives an empty message or a very long one. Which testing would have found this?
options: Fairness testing across user groups
A review of the model card and its limitations
Exception and edge-case testing of inputs
Load testing at expected peak traffic
questions.explanation: Testing edge cases and malformed inputs finds unhandled exceptions that could cause outages or unsafe behavior.

questions.stem: Prompts sent to a model include a user's question and retrieved documents. How should the prompt be structured?
options: Put the retrieved documents before the system instructions so they get more of the model's attention
Clearly separate instructions, user input and retrieved data, and mark data as not to be followed
Let the user write part of the system instructions so answers match what they're looking for
Merge everything into one paragraph so the model reads the question and the context together
questions.explanation: Structured prompts with clear boundaries help the model separate instructions from data. It reduces, but doesn't eliminate, injection risk.

questions.stem: An orchestration harness lets an agent call any API it discovers at runtime. What guardrail is missing?
options: A larger context window for tool descriptions
A faster network between the agent and APIs
An allowlist of approved tools and endpoints
A more detailed model card for the agent
questions.explanation: Agents should only call pre-approved tools and endpoints. Dynamic discovery without allowlisting invites misuse.

references.chapterTitle: OWASP AIVSS Core Agentic AI Security Risks

questions.stem: What should happen when an AI system's guardrail service is unavailable?
options: Switch automatically to a larger model that has its own built-in safety
Disable logging until it recovers, to reduce load on shared systems
Continue serving all requests without checks so users aren't affected
Block or degrade high-risk functions until it recovers
questions.explanation: Guardrails protecting high-risk functions should fail closed; serving without them exposes users and data.

questions.stem: Which content filter belongs on the input side of a customer chatbot?
options: Detection of prompt injection attempts and disallowed requests
Toxicity scoring of the model's answer before it's displayed to the customer
Redaction of personal data in the model's response
Watermarking of the model's generated responses
questions.explanation: Input filters screen what users send; output filters screen what the model returns. Both are needed.

questions.stem: Stress testing shows the AI service returns raw stack traces with internal hostnames under load. What is the issue?
options: Model drift caused by the high request volume
Excessive agency in the service's error handler
Data poisoning through the stress test's inputs
Information disclosure through error messages
questions.explanation: Detailed errors reveal internal details to attackers. Failures should return generic messages and log details internally.

questions.stem: Which guardrail limits damage if an autonomous agent is manipulated into running up costs?
options: Monthly cost reports reviewed by the finance team
Instructions in the agent's prompt to keep costs low
Budget caps and spending limits enforced outside the model
A model with a larger context window and fewer calls
questions.explanation: Hard budget and usage limits enforced by the platform stop runaway spending regardless of what the model is told.

questions.stem: Which accounts should require multi-factor authentication on an AI platform?
options: All human user and administrator accounts
Only accounts that log in from abroad
No accounts, since AI platforms are internal
Only accounts of data scientists
questions.explanation: MFA for every human account, especially administrators, sharply reduces account takeover.

questions.stem: Employees sign in to several AI tools with separate passwords. What improves security and administration?
options: Storing each tool's password in a team password spreadsheet
Federating the tools with the corporate identity provider through SSO
Removing password expiry so employees choose stronger passwords
Asking employees to use one strong password for all of the AI tools
questions.explanation: SSO with a central identity provider gives consistent MFA, faster deprovisioning and central logging.

questions.stem: Why must each agent have a distinct identity?
options: So agents run faster with fewer authentication round trips
So agents can share credentials more easily between tasks
So every action can be attributed to a specific agent
So agents can skip authorization checks for internal calls
questions.explanation: Distinct identities support non-repudiation, per-agent permissions and investigation of who did what.

references.chapterTitle: Designing LLM Systems for Security: Architecture, Controls, and Best Practices

questions.stem: Which credential type is best for a workload that calls a cloud model API?
options: Short-lived tokens obtained through workload identity federation
One API key shared by all workloads, rotated every quarter
A long-lived static API key stored in an environment file
A human user's username and password kept in a vault
questions.explanation: Short-lived, federated credentials avoid stored secrets and expire quickly if stolen.

questions.stem: An agent presents a valid token issued for a different service. What should the receiving API check?
options: Nothing more, since all tokens issued by the company's identity provider are trusted
Only that the token's signature is valid and the signing key is current
Only that the token hasn't expired and was issued within the last hour
The token's audience, so tokens issued for other services are rejected
questions.explanation: Validating audience and issuer prevents tokens meant for one service from being replayed against another.

questions.stem: Mutual TLS is used between two internal AI services. What does it add over standard TLS?
options: It removes the need for encryption between the services
The server also verifies the client's certificate, so both sides are authenticated
It compresses traffic so the services respond faster
It replaces the need for authorization checks on each call, since both sides are trusted
questions.explanation: Standard TLS authenticates the server. Mutual TLS also authenticates the client, establishing both identities.

questions.stem: Which practice supports non-repudiation for actions an agent takes?
options: Letting each agent manage and correct its own log entries
Keeping logs for one day to limit exposure of sensitive data
Signed, tamper-evident logs tied to the agent's unique identity
One shared identity for all agents, with detailed logs
questions.explanation: Non-repudiation needs actions bound to a unique identity and records that can't be altered unnoticed.

questions.stem: Developers store a model API key in a public code repository by mistake. What is the first step?
options: Wait to see whether the key is misused
Revoke and rotate the key immediately
Make the repository private and keep the key
Delete the commit and keep the key
questions.explanation: Once exposed publicly, a key must be treated as compromised. Removing it from history doesn't undo the exposure.

questions.stem: Which entities count as non-human identities in an AI environment?
options: Only the employees who use AI tools in their daily work
Only the vendor support staff who access the platform remotely
Only the external customers who interact with the company's agents
Agents, workloads, services and tools that authenticate to systems
questions.explanation: Non-human identities include anything that authenticates without a person: agents, service accounts, workloads and API clients.

questions.stem: An agent needs to read support tickets but not modify them. How should its access be configured?
options: Read-only access to tickets and nothing else
Full administrator access for flexibility
The same access as the support manager
Write access, with a prompt asking it not to modify tickets
questions.explanation: Least privilege grants only what the task needs. Permissions, not prompts, should prevent modifications.

questions.stem: An agent's API token allows calls to every endpoint in a service, but it uses only two. What should change?
options: Keep the broad scope in case it needs more later
Share the token with other agents that need the API
Rotate the token weekly and keep its current scope
Restrict the token's scope to those two endpoints
questions.explanation: Narrow API scopes limit what a stolen or misused token can do.

questions.stem: A multi-agent system lets a research agent hand tasks to a payments agent. What control prevents misuse of this path?
options: Authorize each payment request against policy and the original requester's rights
Trust all requests from internal agents, since they run inside the company network
Let the research agent approve the payments it requests, since it started the task
Log payments after they settle and review the log at the end of each month
questions.explanation: Each hop should be authorized on its own merits and with the originator's context, preventing privilege escalation through delegation.

references.chapterTitle: OWASP AIVSS Core Agentic AI Security Risks

questions.stem: Who should be able to change an agent's tool permissions in production?
options: The model vendor, through its platform's administration console
Authorized administrators through a reviewed change process
The agent itself, when it determines that a task needs more access
Any end user who needs the agent to perform a new kind of task
questions.explanation: Permission changes are privileged changes that need authorization, review and logging. Agents must never grant themselves access.

questions.stem: Which is an example of an execution boundary for an AI agent?
options: The agent can run code once it explains its reasoning to the user
The agent can run code anywhere it has valid credentials to log in
The agent can run code only in a sandbox with no network access
The agent can run code if its output is reviewed after execution
questions.explanation: Execution boundaries define where and how an agent may act, enforced technically rather than by instruction.

questions.stem: A compromised agent uses its credentials to access other systems on the network. What is this?
options: Hallucination
Model collapse
Data drift
Lateral movement
questions.explanation: Lateral movement is spreading from one compromised point to others. Least privilege and segmentation limit it.

questions.stem: Access to a model's fine-tuning function should be limited to the ML team during business hours from managed devices. Which access model handles these conditions best?
options: Mandatory access control by clearance level only
Discretionary access control
Attribute-based access control
Role-based access control with one role
questions.explanation: ABAC evaluates attributes such as role, time and device posture together, which suits conditional policies.

questions.stem: An agent's broad permissions are justified as "it might need them later." What principle does this violate?
options: Least privilege
Defense in depth
Availability
Non-repudiation
questions.explanation: Least privilege grants access when it's needed, not in anticipation. Excess permissions widen the blast radius of misuse.

questions.stem: Which record should list every agent, service account and API key used by AI systems?
options: The training dataset catalog
A non-human identity inventory with owners
The model card for each AI system, updated at every release
The incident register for AI systems
questions.explanation: An inventory of non-human identities with owners is the basis for reviews, rotation and deprovisioning.

questions.stem: How often should access for AI agents and service accounts be reviewed?
options: Periodically, with owners confirming that each permission is still needed
Only when the agent is first created and its scope is set
Never, since agents don't change roles the way people do
Only after an incident involving that agent or its tools, when the scope is reassessed
questions.explanation: Regular access reviews catch permissions that are no longer needed, for non-human identities as well as people.

questions.stem: When a new agent is created, what should provisioning include?
options: A copy of an existing agent's credentials, so it works with the same systems
An assigned owner, defined purpose, scoped permissions and an expiry or review date
Minimal documentation, since agents can be described later if needed
Administrator access until its actual needs are known, then a later review
questions.explanation: Provisioning with an owner, purpose and scope makes later reviews and deprovisioning possible.

questions.stem: What does identity security posture management (ISPM) help with?
options: Training models faster by allocating GPUs to the right identities and projects automatically
Compressing model weights to reduce storage and transfer costs
Labeling training data more accurately and more consistently
Finding risky identity configurations, such as unused privileges or missing MFA
questions.explanation: ISPM tools continuously assess identities and entitlements for misconfigurations and excess privilege.

questions.stem: A user leaves an AI-assisted session open on a shared device for hours. Which control limits the risk?
options: Watermarking of every output generated during the session
A larger context window for the session
Session time-outs that require re-authentication
Higher rate limits for each session
questions.explanation: Idle and absolute session time-outs reduce the window for someone else to use an unattended session.

questions.stem: Logs show an agent identity hasn't been used in 120 days. What should happen?
options: Confirm with the owner, then disable or remove it if it's no longer needed
Share it with another team that needs similar access
Keep it active, since removing it might break an unknown scheduled job that still depends on it
Increase its permissions so it's ready for future tasks
questions.explanation: Dormant identities are attractive targets. Review and disable unused accounts.

questions.stem: Which audit data best shows how much each agent is consuming from a model platform?
options: The number of developers on each team
GPU utilization logs for the cluster
Per-identity token and request accounting
The total monthly cloud bill for all teams
questions.explanation: Per-identity usage data shows who consumed what, supporting cost control and anomaly detection.

questions.stem: An employee who built several agents leaves the company. What should happen to those agents?
options: Leave the agents running unchanged until they fail
Reassign ownership, then review or disable their credentials
Delete the agents' logs to protect the employee's privacy
Transfer the employee's personal credentials to the agents
questions.explanation: Agents tied to a departing person need new owners, and their access should be reviewed so nothing runs unowned.

questions.stem: Which practice reduces the risk of long-lived credentials for AI services?
options: Using one credential for all AI services
Setting credentials to never expire
Writing credentials into the system's runbooks
Automatic rotation with short expiry periods
questions.explanation: Short-lived, automatically rotated credentials limit the value of a stolen secret.

questions.stem: An access review finds an agent with permissions nobody can explain. What should happen?
options: Add more permissions to be safe, so the agent doesn't fail during tasks
Keep them, since removing them might break something the agent depends on
Ignore them until the next annual review, when the owner can explain them
Remove the unexplained permissions and document the decision
questions.explanation: Unjustified access should be removed. If something breaks, access can be restored with documented approval.

questions.stem: Who should be able to both deploy model changes and approve them in production?
options: No single person; deployment and approval should be separated
The on-call SRE, who is accountable for production stability
The vendor's engineer, who supports the platform
The lead data scientist, who knows the model best
questions.explanation: Separation of duties in AI operations stops one person from pushing unreviewed changes into production.

questions.stem: An AI-specific incident playbook is being written. What should it define first?
options: The public communications templates used to notify customers of incidents
Detailed model architecture and training procedures for each AI system
Roles, escalation paths and decision authority for AI incidents
The list of AI vendors and their support contacts and response times
questions.explanation: Playbooks need clear roles and escalation, including who can take a model offline, before detailed technical steps.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a runbook from a playbook in AI operations?
options: They are the same document, and the two names are used interchangeably in practice
A runbook gives step-by-step procedures; a playbook covers the overall response and decisions
A runbook is written for executives; a playbook is written for engineers on call
A runbook is optional guidance; a playbook is a legal requirement for regulated firms
questions.explanation: Playbooks set the response strategy and decision points; runbooks give the detailed steps to carry out specific tasks, such as rolling back a model.

questions.stem: Guardrail settings for a production assistant differ between two regions, and no one knows why. What practice would prevent this?
options: Configuration management with a tracked baseline and drift detection
Deploying both regions on a larger GPU cluster with shared settings
Turning off guardrails in the region where they block more requests
More frequent retraining of the models deployed in each region
questions.explanation: Configuration baselines and drift detection keep AI settings consistent and make unapproved changes visible.

questions.stem: Before an AI system goes live, operations wants confidence that a human can stop it quickly. What should be tested?
options: The model's training speed and time to redeploy
The marketing and customer communications plan
The vendor's documented service level agreement and support response times
The human override or kill switch, in a realistic drill
questions.explanation: Override mechanisms must be proven to work before they're needed, including who can trigger them and how fast.

questions.stem: A guardrail rejects 15% of user requests in staging, against a release threshold of 5%. What should happen?
options: Disable the guardrail in staging so the release meets its threshold
Raise the threshold to 20% permanently so that future releases of the system aren't held up
Hold the release and investigate whether the guardrail or the model needs tuning
Release anyway, since rejected requests are safer than allowed ones
questions.explanation: A high reject rate signals over-blocking or a problem with the model. Release criteria exist to catch this before users are affected.

questions.stem: Who is responsible for the data feeding a production model, including its quality and permitted use?
options: The model's end users
The data owner
The help desk
The network team
questions.explanation: Clear ownership of data and models is a foundation of AI security operations.

questions.stem: Which is the best way to make sure AI incidents are recognized by the SOC?
options: Wait for the AI vendor to notify the SOC about any incidents
Treat all AI issues as IT help desk tickets handled by support
Rely on users to report unusual answers through a feedback form
Define AI-specific incident categories and detection use cases
questions.explanation: Without defined categories and use cases, AI incidents get missed or misrouted. Detection content should cover AI-specific threats.

questions.stem: Operations staff can view all prompts in the AI logging system, including sensitive ones. What principle applies?
options: Least privilege: limit log access to those who need it
Availability: copy the logs to more locations
Transparency: publish the logs to all employees
Defense in depth: add more logs from more sources
questions.explanation: AI logs can hold sensitive data, so access should be restricted to roles that need it.

questions.stem: Which document sets the minimum security checks every AI release must pass?
options: The privacy notice shown to users
The model card published with each release of the model
A release readiness checklist or definition of done
The vendor's service level agreement
questions.explanation: Release requirements make security checks consistent and auditable before deployment.

questions.stem: Why log retrieved context in a RAG system, not just the prompt and answer?
options: To speed up retrieval by caching documents that are often retrieved
To see whether poisoned or unauthorized documents influenced the answer
To improve the model's accuracy by training on the retrieved context
To reduce storage costs by deduplicating the retrieved documents
questions.explanation: Retrieved content is a common attack path. Logging it lets investigators trace injected or leaked content.

references.chapterTitle: Operational Resilience: Monitoring, Incident Response, and Continuous Improvement

questions.stem: An AI gateway produces logs, but they never reach the SIEM. What is the main consequence?
options: Model training costs rise across the organization's AI projects
Models run more slowly without SIEM integration
AI events can't be correlated with other security events
Users see more errors from the AI gateway
questions.explanation: Correlation in the SIEM connects AI activity to identity, network and endpoint events, which is essential for detection.

questions.stem: Which SOAR action fits an alert that an agent is calling an unapproved external domain?
options: Automatically suspend the agent's credentials and open an incident
Automatically raise the agent's rate limit so its task can finish
Automatically close the alert if the agent is a known internal agent
Automatically retrain the agent's model on the latest data
questions.explanation: SOAR can run predefined containment for high-confidence alerts, with analysts reviewing afterward.

questions.stem: How can threat intelligence improve AI monitoring?
options: By lowering the cost of running AI models and their guardrails
By training the production model on prompts and data collected from known attackers
By replacing the need for detailed logs of AI system activity
By adding known malicious prompts, domains and techniques to detection rules
questions.explanation: Intelligence about current attack techniques, such as new jailbreaks or malicious domains, sharpens detection.

questions.stem: Which metric best signals that a deployed model's behavior is drifting?
options: A change in the model file's size after each redeployment to production
A sustained change in output distributions compared with a baseline
The number of developers online during each shift
The time of day when requests to the model peak
questions.explanation: Tracking output and input distributions against a baseline shows drift before users report problems.

references.chapterTitle: Operational Resilience: Monitoring, Incident Response, and Continuous Improvement

questions.stem: Logs are needed as evidence in a possible legal case. What must be documented?
options: Only the log file names and the systems they came from
Nothing more, since logs are self-explanatory as evidence
Chain of custody showing who collected, handled and stored them
Only the date and time the incident was first detected
questions.explanation: Evidence needs a documented chain of custody so its integrity can be shown in legal or regulatory proceedings.

questions.stem: Which embedding-related event is worth monitoring in a RAG system?
options: The vendor's release notes for each new database version
Unusual bulk insertions or deletions in the vector store
The number of dimensions used for each stored vector
The date and time the vector store was first installed
questions.explanation: Unexpected bulk changes to the vector store can indicate poisoning or data destruction.

references.chapterTitle: Operational Resilience: Monitoring, Incident Response, and Continuous Improvement

questions.stem: Monitoring must catch prompt injection attempts without storing customers' full messages. What approach fits?
options: Run detection on prompts in real time and store masked prompts with detection results
Turn off prompt monitoring entirely and rely on output filtering instead
Store only the model's answers and infer injection attempts from them
Store every prompt in full indefinitely, with access to the stored prompts limited to the SOC team
questions.explanation: Real-time detection gets the signal; masking before storage limits privacy exposure in logs.

questions.stem: Agents act at machine speed. Why is real-time monitoring especially important for them?
options: Agents can't be stopped by anyone once they have started working on a task
Agents always need human approval before each action
Agents don't produce logs that could be reviewed later
Harmful actions can complete before a daily review would notice
questions.explanation: Agents can take many actions quickly, so detection and response must work in near real time.

references.chapterTitle: Operational Resilience: Monitoring, Incident Response, and Continuous Improvement
references.section: Detecting anomalies and potential security incidents in LLM systems

questions.stem: What does a SIEM correlation rule do for AI security?
options: Encrypts logs at rest so attackers who reach the SIEM can't read or alter them
Removes duplicate log entries to reduce storage costs
Links related events across sources to detect patterns a single log wouldn't show
Trains detection models on the collected log data
questions.explanation: Correlation combines signals, such as an unusual login plus abnormal agent tool calls, into higher-confidence detections.

questions.stem: A RAG assistant suddenly cites an unfamiliar internal document that tells users to visit an outside site. What should be investigated?
options: A routine software update to the assistant's front-end application
Expected caching behavior after the knowledge base was reindexed
Normal model creativity, since RAG systems paraphrase documents
Possible poisoning of the knowledge base through injected documents
questions.explanation: Unexpected content in retrieval chains can indicate knowledge base poisoning or indirect injection.

references.chapterTitle: Mapping Trust Boundaries in LLM Architectures

questions.stem: Which signal suggests an agent has more privilege than it should?
options: It answers some questions more slowly than others
It successfully calls administrative APIs outside its task
It returns shorter answers than other agents do
It uses many tokens when summarizing long documents for users
questions.explanation: Successful calls to privileged functions outside the agent's purpose show excess permissions and possible misuse.

questions.stem: A model's GPU utilization spikes and stays at 100% with few user requests. What should be checked?
options: Resource abuse, such as unauthorized workloads or exhaustion attacks
A change in the wording of the model's system prompt
Normal idle behavior while the model is kept warm
A drop in model accuracy caused by recent data drift in production traffic
questions.explanation: Unexplained resource use can signal cryptomining, unauthorized training jobs or denial-of-service attempts.

questions.stem: An unknown identity starts calling the model API with valid credentials. What is the most likely explanation to rule out first?
options: Stolen or leaked credentials
A hallucination
A new model version
Data drift
questions.explanation: Valid credentials used by an unknown party usually mean compromise. Verify, revoke if needed and investigate.

questions.stem: Hash checks show a deployed model file differs from the approved version. What does this indicate?
options: Model drift caused by recent production data and user feedback
A routine log rotation on the model server
A possible integrity compromise of the model artifact
Normal behavior after the server was rebooted
questions.explanation: A mismatch with the approved hash means the artifact changed and must be treated as potentially tampered.

references.chapterTitle: Source Code, Build, and Deployment Management

questions.stem: Which technique helps find threats that existing alerts haven't caught in AI systems?
options: Disabling noisy alerts so analysts can focus on others
Proactive threat hunting based on hypotheses about AI attacks
Rebooting AI servers daily to clear any attacker footholds
Waiting for existing alerts to fire, then tuning them
questions.explanation: Threat hunting looks for signs of attack that rules miss, guided by knowledge of AI attack techniques.

questions.stem: An alert triage queue has hundreds of low-confidence AI alerts daily. How can AI help analysts?
options: Delete low-confidence alerts permanently to reduce the queue
Close all alerts automatically whenever the AI rates them as benign with high confidence
Replace the analysts with an AI agent that handles all triage
Prioritize and summarize alerts, with analysts verifying important ones
questions.explanation: AI-assisted triage reduces load while keeping humans responsible for decisions on important alerts.

questions.stem: A tool connected to an agent begins returning instructions instead of data. What should runtime detection flag?
options: A change in the tool provider's token pricing
Possible tool poisoning or a compromised tool server
Normal behavior for tools that return text
Higher network latency between the agent and the tool's server
questions.explanation: Tool output containing instructions is a sign of tool compromise or injection and should be flagged and contained.

references.chapterTitle: OWASP AIVSS Core Agentic AI Security Risks

questions.stem: Requests to a chatbot show many attempts with slightly different wording, all seeking the system prompt. What is likely happening?
options: The model is drifting away from its baseline
Data in the knowledge base is being poisoned
Users are confused about how the product works
An attacker is probing for system prompt leakage
questions.explanation: Repeated variant attempts suggest deliberate probing. OWASP lists system prompt leakage (LLM07:2025) as a risk.

questions.stem: Which runtime check detects that a model's output contains sensitive internal data?
options: Output scanning for sensitive data patterns and classifications
Data labeling of prompts for later model training
Input rate limiting for each user and session
Model signing and signature verification at each load time
questions.explanation: Scanning outputs for sensitive data catches leakage at runtime regardless of how it reached the model.

questions.stem: An AI pipeline starts pulling data from a new, unregistered source. What should runtime monitoring do?
options: Ignore it, since more data sources usually improve model quality
Increase the pipeline's permissions so the new source loads reliably
Alert, because unapproved sources can introduce poisoned or sensitive data
Delete the pipeline and rebuild it from the last approved version
questions.explanation: Pipelines should only ingest from approved sources. Unregistered sources break integrity and governance.

questions.stem: A widely used ML framework announces a critical vulnerability. What is the first step?
options: Retrain all affected models on the latest version of their data
Turn off every AI system until the vendor releases a patch
Identify which AI systems use the affected version
Wait for a customer to report a problem with one of the AI systems
questions.explanation: Knowing where the vulnerable component runs, through an inventory or AIBOM, comes before prioritizing and patching.

questions.stem: A jailbreak technique published online works against your production assistant. How should it be tracked?
options: As a user complaint to be handled by the support team
As a training data issue to be fixed at the next scheduled retraining of the assistant
As a feature request for the next version of the assistant
As a vulnerability in the register, with an owner, severity and remediation plan
questions.explanation: Model weaknesses such as jailbreak susceptibility belong in the vulnerability register like any other exposure.

questions.stem: Which factor most raises the priority of an AI vulnerability?
options: The affected system is internet-facing and can take actions on real data
The system was built recently, so its code hasn't been reviewed as much
The system uses a popular framework that many other organizations also use
The vulnerability received a lot of attention on social media and in news
questions.explanation: Exposure and potential consequences drive priority more than severity scores alone.

questions.stem: A patch for a model-serving library is available. What should happen before it reaches production?
options: Skip it, since AI serving libraries rarely need patching
Test it in a staging environment that mirrors production
Apply it only to development and wait for issues
Apply it directly to production during peak hours
questions.explanation: Testing patches first avoids outages and confirms the fix works with AI workloads.

questions.stem: Which practice keeps open-source dependencies in AI pipelines from silently becoming vulnerable?
options: Downloading dependencies once at project start and pinning them indefinitely
Continuous dependency scanning with alerts on new vulnerabilities
Using only the oldest stable versions, since they have been tested longest
Removing version numbers from build files so the newest is always used
questions.explanation: Dependency scanning catches newly disclosed vulnerabilities in packages already in use.

references.chapterTitle: Source Code, Build, and Deployment Management

questions.stem: A model can't be patched quickly because retraining takes weeks. What reduces risk meanwhile?
options: Compensating controls such as stricter filtering and restricted access
Removing monitoring from the model to free resources for retraining
Waiting for retraining to finish, with no other changes in the meantime
Publishing the vulnerability details so users can protect themselves
questions.explanation: When a fix takes time, compensating controls reduce exposure until the model can be corrected.

questions.stem: Which metric shows whether AI vulnerability management is improving?
options: Total size of the training data across all models
Total number of models deployed to production
Mean time to remediate high-severity AI findings
Total number of tokens processed each month
questions.explanation: Remediation speed for important findings shows whether the program reduces exposure in practice.

questions.stem: An AI system no one remembers deploying is found exposed to the internet. What practice failed?
options: Security awareness training
Data labeling and quality review processes
Model retraining and evaluation
Asset inventory and posture management
questions.explanation: You can't secure what you don't know about. Asset discovery and inventory are the base of vulnerability management.

questions.stem: Who should own remediation of a vulnerability found in a production model?
options: No one, until it's actually exploited
Whoever reported it, since they understand it best
The security team alone, without the model owner
The model owner, with a tracked due date
questions.explanation: Every finding needs an accountable owner and deadline so it's actually fixed.

questions.stem: A vulnerability is rated medium, but the affected agent can move money. How should priority be set?
options: Lower it, since agents are internal
Keep it medium, since the score is fixed
Raise it, since the business impact is high
Ignore it until the score changes
questions.explanation: Context such as financial impact should raise priority above a generic severity score.

questions.stem: A jailbreak lets users get prohibited content from a public chatbot. What is an appropriate first containment step?
options: Add a targeted block or rate limit and tighten filters while a fix is developed
Announce the jailbreak publicly so users know to avoid it
Delete all chat logs so the prohibited content isn't stored
Retrain the model on refusal examples before taking any other action on the public chatbot
questions.explanation: Contain quickly with targeted controls, preserve evidence and then work on a lasting fix.

references.chapterTitle: Operational Resilience: Monitoring, Incident Response, and Continuous Improvement

questions.stem: Which incident category fits an attacker inserting malicious records into a model's training data?
options: Jailbreak
Data poisoning
Denial of service
Model theft
questions.explanation: Corrupting training data to change model behavior is data poisoning.

questions.stem: A poisoned dataset is discovered in an automated training pipeline. What is the immediate containment step?
options: Pause the pipeline so no further models are trained on it
Delete the pipeline's code and rebuild it from scratch
Notify customers before investigating the scope
Speed up the next training run to replace the model
questions.explanation: Suspending the pipeline stops the problem from spreading to new model versions while you investigate.

references.chapterTitle: Operational Resilience: Monitoring, Incident Response, and Continuous Improvement

questions.stem: A compromised agent keeps reconnecting with new sessions. Which containment action works best?
options: Ask the agent to stop through its system prompt
Revoke its credentials and disable its identity
Lower the agent's temperature to zero
Reboot the laptop of the user who launched it
questions.explanation: Revoking credentials and disabling the identity stops the agent from authenticating again.

questions.stem: A model endpoint is abused, but shutting it down would stop a critical business process. What containment option fits?
options: Delete the model permanently and rebuild the process manually
Leave it fully open until the investigation ends, then decide on containment with the business
Shut down every system in the data center as a precaution
Isolate it to known-good clients and add strict rate limits while investigating
questions.explanation: Containment can be partial: restrict access and throttle to stop abuse while keeping essential service running.

references.chapterTitle: Operational Resilience: Monitoring, Incident Response, and Continuous Improvement

questions.stem: When should data science be involved in an AI incident response?
options: Never, since AI incidents are handled by SecOps alone
Only after the incident is closed, for the final report
When analyzing model behavior, data issues or retraining needs
Only to help write the public statement about the incident
questions.explanation: AI incidents often need data science expertise to understand model behavior and fix data or models.

questions.stem: Before rolling back a vector store to a clean snapshot, what should be preserved?
options: A copy of the current, suspected-poisoned vector store and its logs
Nothing, since the clean snapshot is all that's needed
Only the model's weights from before the incident
Only the user feedback and complaints collected during the incident window
questions.explanation: Preserving the compromised state supports root cause analysis and evidence needs.

references.chapterTitle: Operational Resilience: Monitoring, Incident Response, and Continuous Improvement
references.section: Investigation and analysis techniques for LLM incidents

questions.stem: An AI incident may involve personal data of EU residents. Under the GDPR, how soon must the supervisory authority generally be notified of a qualifying breach?
options: Within 30 days, once the investigation has concluded
Within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, where feasible
Within one year, as part of the annual compliance report
Only if affected customers complain to the organization
questions.explanation: GDPR Article 33 requires notification without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours, unless the breach is unlikely to result in risk to individuals.

questions.stem: Which incident type is model extraction?
options: Exhausting compute resources with costly requests
Corrupting training data with malicious samples before training
Bypassing safety filters with crafted prompts
Theft of model functionality through systematic querying
questions.explanation: Model extraction copies a model's behavior by querying it, which is a form of IP theft.

questions.stem: What should a forensic timeline for an AI incident include?
options: The model's training dates and the versions released during the year
Only the time the incident was reported and the time it was closed
Time-stamped events from prompts, tool calls, data changes and deployments
The vendor's maintenance windows and outage history for the period
questions.explanation: A timeline across AI and infrastructure events shows how the attack unfolded.

references.chapterTitle: Operational Resilience: Monitoring, Incident Response, and Continuous Improvement
references.section: Investigation and analysis techniques for LLM incidents

questions.stem: Investigators find an agent was manipulated through content in a shared document. What is the root cause to fix?
options: The shared document was too long for the agent's context window
The agent responded too slowly, so the user retried with altered text
The user typed the request too quickly for input validation to run
Untrusted document content was allowed to steer a privileged agent
questions.explanation: Root cause analysis should identify the design weakness, here untrusted content reaching a privileged agent, not just the symptom.

questions.stem: A model is retrained after poisoning, but the same backdoor appears again. What is the most likely reason?
options: The model card wasn't updated to describe the backdoor's trigger
The model was trained for too few epochs to unlearn the backdoor
The poisoned data wasn't fully removed from the training set
A faulty GPU corrupted the retrained weights during the training run
questions.explanation: Eradication fails if any poisoned data remains. Trace lineage and validate the cleaned dataset before retraining.

questions.stem: Why should a malicious prompt found during an investigation be added to a test suite?
options: To replace logging of prompts in production
To confirm the fix works and catch regressions later
To raise token usage so monitoring can be calibrated
To train new analysts on real attacker techniques
questions.explanation: Turning attack samples into regression tests verifies remediation and prevents reintroduction.

questions.stem: What is the main goal of reconstructing the kill chain in an AI incident?
options: To understand each step of the attack and where controls failed
To prepare public statements explaining the incident to customers
To identify which individuals were responsible for the failure
To speed up model retraining by reusing the attack's data
questions.explanation: Mapping each attack stage shows which controls failed and where to strengthen defenses.

questions.stem: An investigation finds attackers exploited an unpatched model-serving library. What is part of eradication?
options: Only deleting old logs so the attacker can't learn from them later
Only restarting the model-serving service to clear the attacker's session
Only resetting the passwords of users who were active during the attack
Patching the library and checking for any persistence the attacker left
questions.explanation: Eradication removes the vulnerability and any foothold, such as backdoors or new accounts, before recovery.

questions.stem: Which framework helps describe the techniques used in an AI attack in a common language?
options: MITRE ATLAS
The EU AI Act risk tiers
NIST AI RMF Govern function
ISO/IEC 42001
questions.explanation: ATLAS catalogs adversary tactics and techniques against AI systems, useful for describing and comparing attacks.

questions.stem: A forensic copy of model weights is needed for analysis. How should it be handled?
options: Store it on an investigator's personal laptop
Hash it, store it securely and analyze a working copy
Analyze the only copy directly to save time
Email it to the investigation team so they can each review it promptly
questions.explanation: Preserving an original with a hash and working on copies keeps evidence intact.

questions.stem: After eradication, testing shows the model now refuses many legitimate requests. What should happen?
options: Release it anyway, since blocking too much is safer than too little
Remove the new safety controls so legitimate requests are answered again, then monitor for misuse
Tune the fix and retest before reintroduction, balancing safety and usefulness
Retire the model immediately and rebuild the feature without AI
questions.explanation: Safety regression testing checks both that attacks are blocked and that normal use still works.

questions.stem: Which backup is most important for restoring a RAG assistant after its knowledge base is corrupted?
options: Verified snapshots of the vector store and its source documents
Screenshots of the chat interface showing earlier answers
The model's weights and its most recent fine-tuning data
The user feedback collected before the corruption occurred
questions.explanation: Restoring retrieval needs clean copies of the vector store or the verified documents to rebuild it.

references.chapterTitle: Operational Resilience: Monitoring, Incident Response, and Continuous Improvement

questions.stem: Which checkpoint should be used to restore a model after an incident?
options: A checkpoint from a different model
The newest checkpoint, whatever its state
The most recent checkpoint verified as clean
A random checkpoint
questions.explanation: Recovery must start from a known-good state, verified as created before the compromise.

questions.stem: What should a post-incident review for an AI incident produce?
options: A communication plan for customers and the press
A list of the people responsible, for follow-up by HR
A proposal for a new model architecture for the system
Lessons learned and assigned actions to improve controls
questions.explanation: Reviews should be blameless and focused on improvements, with owners and due dates for actions.

questions.stem: What is a TTP register used for after AI incidents?
options: Listing third-party vendors and their security contacts
Recording attacker tactics, techniques and procedures seen, to improve detection
Recording model token prices and usage for budgeting
Tracking training time and GPU costs for each AI project across the organization each quarter
questions.explanation: Capturing observed TTPs helps tune detection and prepare for similar attacks.

questions.stem: A business process depends on an AI model. What should the business continuity plan define?
options: The model's accuracy targets and how they will be measured
A plan to retrain the model from scratch if it is ever taken offline by the vendor
The vendor's support contacts and escalation procedures only
A fallback way to run the process if the model is unavailable or unsafe
questions.explanation: Continuity planning needs a manual or alternative process for when AI must be taken offline.

questions.stem: Dependency mapping shows an AI service relies on an external vector database, an identity provider and a model API. Why does this matter for recovery?
options: Recovery must restore or work around each dependency, not just the model
Only the model needs restoring, since it holds the system's logic
Dependencies don't affect the availability of the AI service itself
