Managed dependencies recover automatically, so they need no plan
questions.explanation: AI services fail if any critical dependency fails. Recovery plans should cover each one.

questions.stem: A model is being retired. What must happen to customer data it was fine-tuned on?
options: Transfer it to the model vendor, which will manage its retention
Handle it under retention rules, deleting it and derived artifacts where required
Publish an anonymized version of it for research use
Keep it indefinitely in case a future model needs it for training or for evaluation
questions.explanation: Decommissioning includes disposing of data and derived artifacts according to retention and privacy obligations.

questions.stem: A circuit breaker has tripped and stopped an agent. What should happen before it is reset?
options: Raise its threshold so it doesn't trip again under similar conditions
Remove the circuit breaker, since it disrupted the process
Investigate the cause and confirm it's safe to resume
Reset it immediately so the business process can resume
questions.explanation: A tripped breaker signals a problem. Resetting without understanding it risks repeating the harm.

questions.stem: How should recovery procedures for AI systems be validated?
options: By reviewing the vendor's recovery documentation each year
By testing them only after a real incident has occurred
By regularly testing restores and failovers in practice
By confirming each night that backup jobs reported success
questions.explanation: Untested recovery plans often fail. Regular restore and failover tests prove they work.

questions.stem: In STRIDE, an agent impersonating another agent to gain its permissions is which threat category?
options: Repudiation
Denial of service
Information disclosure
Spoofing
questions.explanation: Spoofing is pretending to be another identity. Strong per-agent authentication counters it.

references.chapterTitle: Architecture (A2): SDL Activities and Best Practices

questions.stem: In STRIDE, an agent denying it made a harmful change, with no logs to prove otherwise, is which category?
options: Repudiation
Tampering
Elevation of privilege
Spoofing
questions.explanation: Repudiation is being able to deny an action. Tamper-evident logging tied to identities addresses it.

references.chapterTitle: Architecture (A2): SDL Activities and Best Practices

questions.stem: Which threat actor is most likely to try to steal a startup's proprietary model weights?
options: A curious user exploring the product's chatbot features
A competitor or an insider seeking commercial gain
An academic researcher studying public model benchmarks
An automated search engine crawler indexing the startup's site
questions.explanation: Model weights are valuable IP. Competitors, criminal groups and insiders have motive to steal them.

references.chapterTitle: The AI Threat Landscape: Dissecting the Risks and Attack Vectors

questions.stem: A compromised automation agent with valid credentials acts against the organization. How should a threat model classify it?
options: A natural disaster
An external DDoS attack
A non-human insider threat
A physical intrusion
questions.explanation: Agents with legitimate access behave like insiders when compromised or manipulated. Threat models should include non-human insiders.

references.chapterTitle: OWASP AIVSS Core Agentic AI Security Risks

questions.stem: Which OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025) entry covers manipulation of pre-training, fine-tuning or embedding data?
options: LLM09: Misinformation
LLM01: Prompt Injection
LLM05: Improper Output Handling
LLM04: Data and Model Poisoning
questions.explanation: LLM04:2025 covers poisoning of training, fine-tuning and embedding data, as well as tampered models.

questions.stem: A voice assistant receives audio with hidden commands people can't hear. Which threat class is this?
options: Data residency violation by the audio processor
Adversarial input against a multimodal or speech system
Membership inference against the speech model
Model extraction through repeated voice queries to the assistant
questions.explanation: Multimodal systems can be attacked through crafted audio or images that carry hidden commands or perturbations.

questions.stem: Which source gives threat intelligence specific to attacks on AI systems, including real-world case studies?
options: MITRE ATLAS
The CVSS calculator
ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A
The OSI model
questions.explanation: ATLAS documents AI-specific tactics, techniques and case studies drawn from real attacks and red team work.

questions.stem: A threat model for a RAG system lists only external hackers. What is missing?
options: Nothing, since external hackers are the main risk to RAG systems
Only nation-state actors targeting the organization's suppliers
Only physical threats to the data center that hosts the system
Insiders, compromised content sources and supply chain threats
questions.explanation: Threat models should cover all actors and paths: insiders, poisoned sources, dependencies and agents, not just outside attackers.

questions.stem: Which NIST publication provides a taxonomy and terminology for adversarial machine learning attacks and mitigations?
options: NIST SP 800-88
NIST SP 800-37
NIST AI 100-2
NIST SP 800-63
questions.explanation: NIST AI 100-2 sets out a taxonomy of adversarial ML, covering attacks such as evasion, poisoning and privacy attacks on predictive and generative AI.

questions.stem: Where should security activities fit in the AI development lifecycle?
options: At every stage, from data collection through monitoring
Only after an incident, when weaknesses become clear
Only during data labeling, where most risk is introduced
Only at the end of development, in a pre-release review
questions.explanation: Secure AIDLC builds security into each stage, which is cheaper and more effective than adding it at the end.

references.chapterTitle: Architecture (A2): SDL Activities and Best Practices

questions.stem: A prompt template change is pushed straight to production without review. What practice should apply?
options: A review only after users report changes in the assistant's behavior
Change management with review, testing and approval for prompt changes
A review once a year as part of the application's annual audit
No formal process, since prompt templates are just configuration text
questions.explanation: Prompts change system behavior and can weaken safety, so they need the same change control as code.

questions.stem: Which practice lets a team roll back to the exact retrieval index used last week?
options: Storing the index without metadata to keep its size small
Keeping only the latest index to avoid confusion between versions
Versioning retrieval indexes alongside models and prompts
Rebuilding the index from scratch from current documents each time
questions.explanation: Versioned indexes let you restore a known-good state and compare behavior between versions.

questions.stem: In a blue/green deployment of a new model, what happens?
options: Traffic moves from the old environment to an identical new one, with quick switch-back if needed
The new model receives copies of live traffic, but its answers are never shown to users
Both models answer each request, and the application averages their two answers
A small share of users gets the new model first, and the share grows over several days
questions.explanation: Blue/green runs two full environments and switches traffic between them, enabling fast rollback. Gradual exposure is canary; mirrored traffic is shadow.

references.chapterTitle: Designing an Enterprise ML Architecture with AWS ML Services

questions.stem: Developers can push code directly to the branch that deploys models. Which control is missing?
options: Larger GPU quotas for the training jobs
Protected branches with required reviews
Faster build servers for the pipeline
More detailed logging of user prompts
questions.explanation: Branch protection and required reviews prevent unreviewed changes from reaching production.

references.chapterTitle: Source Code, Build, and Deployment Management

questions.stem: Development, staging and production share one set of credentials and one data store. What risk does this create?
options: Better model accuracy, because all environments share the same data
Lower costs, with no meaningful downside for a small team
Faster testing, because developers can use realistic production data
A compromise or mistake in development can reach production data and models
questions.explanation: Environment separation keeps test activity and weaker dev controls from affecting production.

questions.stem: Which check belongs in the CI pipeline for an AI application?
options: Manual approval of the grammar and spelling in every developer's commit message
Automated security tests, including prompt injection test cases
A check that developers committed during working hours
A test of the office network speed before each build
questions.explanation: Automated tests, including AI-specific attacks, catch regressions on each change.

questions.stem: A model update is rolled out, and safety metrics worsen. What should the deployment process do?
options: Roll back automatically or on approval when thresholds are crossed
Increase traffic to the new model to gather more data quickly
Continue the rollout and review the safety metrics next week
Disable the safety metrics, since they may be overly sensitive
questions.explanation: Defined rollback triggers limit harm when a release degrades safety or quality.

questions.stem: APIs between AI components are added without authentication because they're internal. What principle is violated?
options: Data minimization for internal APIs
Transparency about internal API usage
Availability of internal API endpoints between components
Zero Trust: authenticate and authorize every request
questions.explanation: Internal networks can be breached. Zero Trust requires authentication and authorization on every call.

references.chapterTitle: Designing LLM Systems for Security: Architecture, Controls, and Best Practices

questions.stem: Which document should record why a change to a production model was approved?
options: The vendor's release notes for the new version of the model
The model card's intended-use section
The change record, with risk assessment, tests and approver
The user manual for the application
questions.explanation: Change records provide an audit trail of what changed, why, how it was tested and who approved it.

questions.stem: Who should be able to modify the training pipeline's configuration?
options: The models being trained, which can tune their own settings
External contractors, without review, for faster changes
Anyone with read access to the pipeline's repository, so fixes aren't delayed by reviews
Authorized engineers through reviewed changes, under least privilege
questions.explanation: Pipeline configuration controls what gets built; access should be limited and changes reviewed.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports trust in an AI vendor's security claims?
options: Independent certifications and recent assessment reports
The vendor's sponsorship of major security conferences
The vendor's size, headcount and years in business
Testimonials and case studies published on the vendor's website
questions.explanation: Third-party certifications and assessments provide independent evidence; marketing claims don't.

questions.stem: Before buying an AI product, what should be agreed about data ownership?
options: Only the product's price and the payment schedule
Who owns inputs, outputs and any models trained on customer data
Only the vendor's support hours and guaranteed response times
Only where the vendor may place the buyer's logo
questions.explanation: Ownership of inputs, outputs and derived models must be settled in contract to avoid IP and privacy disputes.

questions.stem: A vendor provides a model with a signed manifest. What does verifying the signature confirm?
options: The model is free of bias against protected groups
The model is accurate enough for production use
The manifest came from the vendor and hasn't been altered
The model is licensed for every use the buyer intends
questions.explanation: Signatures prove origin and integrity, not quality, fairness or license fitness.

questions.stem: An AI product includes custom hardware accelerators. What should the AI-BOM cover?
options: Only the training data sources and their licenses
Only the model weights and their file hashes
Hardware and firmware components, along with software, models and data
Only the software libraries and their versions, since hardware is covered elsewhere
questions.explanation: AI-BOMs can include hardware dependencies, since firmware and accelerators are part of the supply chain.

questions.stem: Which OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025) risk covers vulnerable third-party models, datasets and components?
options: LLM07: System Prompt Leakage
LLM03: Supply Chain
LLM06: Excessive Agency
LLM10: Unbounded Consumption
questions.explanation: LLM03:2025 covers risks from third-party models, data, libraries and services in the LLM supply chain.

questions.stem: An AI vendor is acquired by a company in another country. What should the customer reassess?
options: Nothing, since the product's name and features are unchanged
Only the invoice address and payment details for the contract
Only the vendor's branding on the product and its documentation
Data residency, ownership and contract terms under the new owner
questions.explanation: Ownership changes can affect where data goes, who can access it and which laws apply.

questions.stem: What should procurement require before an AI vendor's model goes into production?
options: Documented testing results, including security and bias evaluations
A free trial period long enough to evaluate the features
A discount in exchange for signing a multi-year contract
A published case study from another customer in the industry
questions.explanation: Evidence of testing shows how a model performs and fails, supporting the risk decision.

questions.stem: A model's provenance record lists its training data sources, base model and fine-tuning steps. What is this used for?
options: Making the model run faster in production
Establishing the model's pedigree and supporting trust decisions
Encrypting the model's weights while stored
Removing the need for further security and bias testing before use
questions.explanation: Provenance shows where a model came from and how it was built, which supports security, legal and quality review.

questions.stem: A vendor won't say whether it trains on customer prompts. What is the main risk?
options: Prompts will be processed more slowly during busy periods
Billing will be harder to predict from month to month
Model outputs will be shorter than the vendor advertises
Confidential data could end up in the vendor's models
questions.explanation: Unclear data use terms risk leaking confidential information into shared models. Get it in writing.

questions.stem: Which practice reduces risk from a single AI vendor's outage or contract change?
options: Storing data only in the vendor's proprietary format
Signing the longest contract available for better pricing
Planning exit options and keeping portable data and prompts
Reducing internal AI expertise to lower operating costs
questions.explanation: Exit planning and portability reduce lock-in and allow switching if a vendor fails or changes terms.

questions.stem: An open-source model package on a public registry has a name one letter off from a popular model. What risk is this?
options: Typosquatting to deliver a malicious model
Excessive agency in the package
A data residency violation
Model drift after installation and first use
questions.explanation: Attackers publish look-alike names hoping users install the wrong package. Verify publishers and hashes.

references.chapterTitle: Source Code, Build, and Deployment Management

questions.stem: Which document authorizes a red team to test a production AI system and sets limits on what they may do?
options: Written rules of engagement signed by an authorized owner
An email from the red team lead confirming the test dates
A ticket in the application team's backlog describing the test
A verbal agreement with the developer who built the system
questions.explanation: Rules of engagement set scope, methods, limits and contacts, and protect both testers and the organization.

questions.stem: Red teamers want to test whether a RAG assistant leaks other users' data. Which test fits?
options: Check the interface's accessibility and color contrast settings
Count the tokens in each answer and compare them with the limit
Craft queries that try to retrieve documents outside the tester's permissions
Measure the assistant's response time under many concurrent queries from different users
questions.explanation: Authorization testing for RAG checks whether retrieval respects each user's access rights.

references.chapterTitle: Diving Deep: Profiles of the Top 10 LLM Security Risks

questions.stem: Why should AI red teaming combine automated tools with human testers?
options: Human testers are always more effective than tools, so tools only add cost
Tools give scale and coverage; humans find creative, context-specific attacks
Combining them is required by regulation, but adds little practical value
Automated tools are always more thorough than human testers, so humans only review
questions.explanation: Automated testing covers many known patterns; human testers find novel attacks and business-logic flaws.

questions.stem: Red teamers plan to test an agent that can send real emails. How should they avoid harm?
options: Send test emails to a small group of real customers who agreed to beta testing
Disable logging during the test so test emails don't trigger alerts
Test without telling the system owner, so the results are realistic
Test in a controlled environment or with safeguards such as sandboxed recipients
questions.explanation: Testing agentic actions needs safeguards so tests don't cause real-world harm.

questions.stem: Which test checks whether an LLM application safely handles model output passed to a web page?
options: Trying to make the model output script content that the page renders
Checking that the model's license allows output on public web pages
Measuring the model's accuracy on questions about the web page
Counting the number of API calls the page makes for each answer
questions.explanation: Improper output handling can lead to cross-site scripting when output is rendered unsanitized.

questions.stem: A red team uses an LLM to generate thousands of jailbreak variants. What is this an example of?
options: Model extraction
Data poisoning
AI-assisted security testing
Shadow AI
questions.explanation: AI tools can generate and mutate attacks at scale, broadening test coverage.

questions.stem: What should a red team test for in a system that uses an LLM to decide which tool to call?
options: Whether the tool names in the system prompt are spelled correctly
Whether it selects and calls tools quickly enough to keep response times acceptable for users
Whether each tool has up-to-date documentation for developers
Whether manipulated input can make it call unintended or unauthorized tools
questions.explanation: Tool selection is an attack surface. Tests should try to steer the model into misusing tools.

references.chapterTitle: OWASP AIVSS Core Agentic AI Security Risks

questions.stem: Which objective best describes the purpose of an AI red team exercise?
options: Prove that the system has no remaining vulnerabilities
Find weaknesses under realistic attack conditions before adversaries do
Generate evidence for marketing claims about security
Collect attack data so the model can be trained to resist the same attacks in the future
questions.explanation: Red teaming seeks real weaknesses; it can't prove their absence.

questions.stem: Testers try to get a chatbot to reveal its system prompt. Which risk are they testing?
options: Model collapse
Data poisoning
Supply chain compromise
System prompt leakage
questions.explanation: OWASP lists system prompt leakage (LLM07:2025). Prompts shouldn't hold secrets, since they can be extracted.

questions.stem: Which scenario tests a multi-agent system's resilience to one compromised agent?
options: Injecting malicious messages from one agent and observing whether others act on them
Reviewing each agent's description and its documented responsibilities
Renaming the agents so attackers can't predict which one to target
Measuring total token usage across all of the agents during a normal workload for a full week
questions.explanation: Testing agent-to-agent trust shows whether one compromised agent can cascade harm.

references.chapterTitle: OWASP AIVSS Core Agentic AI Security Risks

questions.stem: A jailbreak works in 2 of 50 attempts. How should exploitability be reported?
options: Leave it out of the report, since the success rate is low
Report it as working every time, to be conservative
Report the success rate with the conditions and steps to reproduce
Report it as not reproducible, since it failed in 48 of the 50 attempts made
questions.explanation: LLM attacks are often probabilistic. Reporting the rate and conditions gives an accurate picture of risk.

questions.stem: Which finding is most severe?
options: A spelling mistake in the chatbot's welcome message
An injection that makes an agent transfer funds without approval
A chatbot that gives the wrong store opening time
Slow responses from the customer chatbot during off-peak hours each night
questions.explanation: Severity weighs impact: unauthorized financial actions far outweigh inaccuracies and cosmetic issues.

questions.stem: A finding maps to MITRE ATLAS techniques and an OWASP LLM category. Why include both?
options: They give common references that help others understand and compare the finding
They're required for the finding to be considered valid
They replace the need for detailed reproduction steps
They determine the finding's severity score automatically, so analysts don't have to rate it
questions.explanation: Mapping to shared frameworks makes findings easier to understand, compare and track across teams.

questions.stem: What should evidence for an AI red team finding include?
options: The tester's personal assessment of how serious and how likely the finding is
A screenshot of the most damaging response
Exact prompts, responses, timestamps, model version and configuration
A short summary of the attack in plain language
questions.explanation: Detailed evidence lets developers reproduce and fix the issue and lets reviewers verify it.

questions.stem: A model gives biased hiring recommendations, but no security boundary is crossed. How should it be reported?
options: As not reportable, since it doesn't cross a security boundary or expose any data
As a network configuration issue for the infrastructure team
As a critical remote code execution flaw in the model
As a significant responsible AI and compliance risk, routed to the right owners
questions.explanation: Not every important finding is a security vulnerability. Bias in hiring carries legal and ethical risk and should be routed accordingly.

references.chapterTitle: Bias, Explainability, Privacy, and Adversarial Attacks

questions.stem: Engineers need to fix a prompt injection finding. What should their version of the report emphasize?
options: Business impact in dollar terms, with no technical detail
Root cause, reproduction steps and recommended technical fixes
The history of prompt injection research and notable incidents
The tester's background and the tools the red team used
questions.explanation: Technical audiences need what failed, how to reproduce it and how to fix it.

questions.stem: A finding can only be exploited by an authenticated administrator. How does this affect its rating?
options: It makes the finding irrelevant to the report
It has no effect on how the finding is rated
It lowers likelihood, but impact still needs assessment
It automatically makes the finding critical, since administrators hold the most access
questions.explanation: Required privileges lower exploitability, but impact and insider risk still matter.

questions.stem: Validation shows a reported finding can't be reproduced after many attempts. What should happen?
options: Record it with the evidence and conditions, and keep watching for recurrence
Ask the tester to explain why the finding can't be reproduced
Mark it as critical until someone can prove it was a false positive
Delete it from the report, since the system appears to have been fixed
questions.explanation: Non-deterministic systems can make findings intermittent. Keep the evidence and watch for recurrence.

questions.stem: Which finding is a model limitation rather than a security vulnerability?
options: An attacker extracts customer data through a crafted prompt
An agent runs shell commands supplied by users
A token leak allows unauthorized API calls
The model sometimes misreads handwriting in scanned forms
questions.explanation: Recognition errors without a security impact are limitations. The others breach confidentiality, integrity or authorization.

references.chapterTitle: Do Language Models Dream of Electric Sheep?

questions.stem: Two findings have the same technical severity, but one affects a customer-facing payment flow. How should they be ranked?
options: Rank the other finding higher, since it was found first
Rank the payment flow finding higher because of business impact
Rank them by which one is cheaper to fix
Rank them equally, since their severity scores are the same
questions.explanation: Business context should adjust priority when technical scores are similar.

questions.stem: After an assessment, what should the final report give executives?
options: Overall risk posture, top issues and decisions or resources needed
Raw output from each testing tool
Source code of the tools used during testing
Every prompt and response used in testing, in full detail
questions.explanation: Executives need a concise view of risk and what they must decide or fund.

questions.stem: Which mitigation makes a model more robust to adversarial examples?
options: Reducing logging of model inputs
Increasing the model's context window and input size
Adversarial training with crafted examples
Publishing a detailed model card
questions.explanation: Adversarial training exposes the model to attack examples during training to improve robustness. It helps, but doesn't eliminate the risk.

questions.stem: Which mitigation best reduces the risk of poisoned data entering training?
options: Raising the learning rate during training
Data validation and provenance tracking for every source
Moving to a larger model with more parameters and broader training
Training for more epochs on each dataset
questions.explanation: Validating data and tracking where it comes from stops much poisoning before training.

questions.stem: A mitigation would block an attack but break a feature customers rely on. How should the team decide?
options: Never change features that customers rely on
Always choose the strongest security control, whatever the impact
Let the affected customers vote on the change
Weigh risk reduction against business impact and consider alternatives
questions.explanation: Mitigation decisions balance security with business needs; alternatives may achieve both.

questions.stem: After a fix is deployed, how should residual risk be handled?
options: Monitor for recurrence and record the remaining risk with an owner
Assume the risk is gone now that the fix has been deployed
Remove the related alerts so they don't create noise
Close the finding once the fix is deployed, without verification
questions.explanation: Fixes rarely remove all risk. Monitoring and documented ownership keep residual risk visible.

references.chapterTitle: Creating Trustworthy AI: A Lifecycle Risk Management Framework

questions.stem: Which mitigation limits the impact of a successful prompt injection against an agent?
options: More frequent retraining on recent prompt injection examples
Restricting the agent's tools and permissions to the minimum needed
A more detailed system prompt that warns about manipulation
A larger context window so instructions are not truncated
questions.explanation: Limiting what the agent can do caps the damage injection can cause, even when it succeeds.

questions.stem: Which control reduces the risk of generated code executing harmful commands?
options: Asking the model in its system prompt to write only safe, non-destructive code
Running it on a faster CPU so it finishes sooner
Logging the code after it runs for later review
Running it in a sandbox with restricted network and file access
questions.explanation: Sandboxing contains whatever the code does, regardless of how it was generated.

questions.stem: A mitigation reduces an attack's success rate from 40% to 5%. What should happen next?
options: Stop testing the system now that the rate is low
Declare the risk eliminated and close the finding, since the rate dropped by most of the way
Decide whether 5% is acceptable or add layered controls, then monitor
Remove the mitigation, since some attacks still succeed
questions.explanation: Partial reductions leave residual risk. Decide whether it's within appetite and add layers if not.

questions.stem: Which validation step confirms a mitigation hasn't introduced new problems?
options: Regression testing of existing functionality and security tests
Reading the vendor's release notes for the filter
Asking a sample of users whether they noticed any changes in how the system behaves
Checking that the model's file size hasn't changed
questions.explanation: Regression tests confirm both that the fix works and that nothing else broke.

questions.stem: Several mitigations are proposed for one risk. Which should usually come first?
options: The most expensive one, since it's usually the most thorough
The one proposed most recently by the team
The one that's easiest to explain to leadership
The one with the most risk reduction for reasonable effort
questions.explanation: Prioritize by risk reduced relative to effort and feasibility.

questions.stem: A watermarking mitigation is added to detect leaked generated content. What is a known limitation?
options: Watermarks stop the model from generating content
Watermarks can be weakened by editing or paraphrasing
Watermarks always reveal the identity of the user
Watermarks make generated text unreadable to people
questions.explanation: Watermarks help with detection, but heavy editing or paraphrasing can remove or weaken them.

questions.stem: Which mitigation addresses unbounded consumption by API clients?
options: Publishing monthly usage statistics
Encrypting the model's weights at rest and in transit
Rate limits, quotas and caps on output length
Adding more training data to the model
questions.explanation: Limiting requests, tokens and output size per client counters resource exhaustion (OWASP LLM10:2025).

lessons.summary: AI is the broad field; machine learning learns patterns from data; deep learning uses many-layered neural networks. Expect scenarios built on classic ML, not only LLMs.
points: Supervised learning trains on labeled data (classification, regression). Unsupervised finds structure without labels (clustering, anomaly detection). Reinforcement learning optimizes actions through rewards.
CNNs suit spatial data such as images. RNNs handle sequences but have largely given way to transformers, which use attention and power modern LLMs.
Evolutionary computation (for example genetic algorithms) searches for solutions through mutation and selection rather than gradient training.
GPUs and TPUs accelerate the parallel matrix math of training and inference. Model weights and accelerator memory are high-value assets to protect.
traps: Treating every AI question as an LLM question. Fraud classifiers and anomaly detectors are AI too.
lessons.tip: Match the paradigm to the data: labels mean supervised, no labels mean unsupervised, a reward signal means reinforcement.

lessons.summary: Generative models predict the next token. Most enterprise patterns combine a foundation model with retrieval, adapters, tools and memory, and each adds attack surface.
points: RAG retrieves current documents at query time and places them in the context window, so knowledge updates without retraining.
Fine-tuning changes weights. LoRA and other PEFT methods train small adapter parameters, which is cheaper and easier to swap.
Embeddings are vectors that capture meaning. Vector databases run similarity search over them. The context window is everything the model can see at once, measured in tokens.
Agents combine a model with tools, memory and a loop. Session persistence and long-term memory let a single injected instruction survive across turns.
traps: Choosing fine-tuning to keep facts current. RAG is the answer for freshness; fine-tuning is for style, format or behavior.
lessons.tip: Anything in the context window can steer the output, so treat retrieved text, tool results and memory as untrusted input.

lessons.summary: Models are probabilistic and degrade over time. Know the difference between reliability limits, drift and collapse, and how to measure them.
points: Hallucinations are confident, ungrounded output. Non-determinism comes from sampling settings such as temperature. Neither requires an attacker.
Data drift means input distributions change. Concept or model drift means the relationship between inputs and outcomes changes. Behavioral drift shows up when a provider updates a model.
Model collapse is the loss of quality and diversity when models are trained repeatedly on AI-generated data.
Precision matters when false positives are costly; recall matters when misses are costly. F1 balances them. LLMs also need task-specific evaluations and benchmarks.
traps: Calling a hallucination a security vulnerability. It is a reliability limitation unless it crosses a security boundary.
lessons.tip: The higher the impact of a decision, the more the exam expects human review over automated execution.

lessons.summary: Model quality and privacy both start with data handling: what you collect, how you prepare it and whether you can prove where it came from.
points: Structured data has a fixed schema; unstructured data (documents, images, chat logs) is harder to classify and filter.
Lifecycle stages: acquisition, extraction, cleaning, transformation, labeling. Errors or tampering at any stage flow into the model.
Quality dimensions include accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness and relevance.
Privacy techniques: masking, tokenization, k-anonymity, synthetic data and differential privacy each trade utility for protection differently.
traps: Assuming pseudonymized or tokenized data is no longer personal data. If it can be re-linked, it still is.
lessons.tip: Provenance questions ask one thing: where did this data come from, and can you prove it?

lessons.summary: AI threats are best sorted by where in the lifecycle they strike: training time, inference time or through connected tools.
points: Zero Trust for AI: never implicitly trust prompts, retrieved content, model output or agent requests; verify each one.
Direct prompt injection comes from the user. Indirect injection hides in content the model reads, such as emails, web pages or files. Jailbreaking bypasses safety behavior.
Evasion crafts inputs at inference to cause misclassification. Poisoning corrupts training data. Model inversion and membership inference extract information about training data.
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications lists application risks. NIST provides the AI RMF and an adversarial ML taxonomy. MITRE ATLAS catalogs adversary tactics and techniques.
traps: Mixing up evasion (inference time) and poisoning (training time).
lessons.tip: Ask when the attacker acts and what they touch; that usually identifies the attack.

lessons.summary: Effective safeguards are enforced outside the model, where they can't be talked out of working.
points: Guardrails validate inputs and filter outputs for injection patterns, toxicity and sensitive data.
Responsible AI principles include transparency, explainability, fairness and awareness of bias.
Model verification uses evaluation sets, red teaming and signature checks on artifacts.
Isolation separates AI environments through sandboxes, network segmentation and tenant separation.
traps: Treating a system prompt instruction as a security control. It can be overridden by injection.
lessons.tip: Prefer deterministic controls (authorization, filters, scopes) over asking the model to behave.

lessons.summary: Use cases set the stakes. The same model needs very different oversight in a marketing tool and a credit decision.
points: Business and development uses include copilots, summarization and code generation, which can introduce insecure code or license issues.
Healthcare involves PHI and high-stakes decisions. Finance uses AI for fraud and credit, where fairness and explainability are regulated.
Law enforcement uses such as biometric identification are high risk, and some are prohibited under the EU AI Act.
Security operations use AI for alert triage, threat intelligence, vulnerability prioritization and automation, with human approval for destructive actions.
traps: Letting AI-generated code skip normal review and testing.
lessons.tip: Higher stakes for people mean more oversight, documentation and testing.

lessons.summary: Governance starts with knowing what AI you have, then applying frameworks and regulations proportionate to risk.
points: EU AI Act tiers: prohibited practices, high-risk (for example employment, credit, critical infrastructure), limited risk with transparency duties, and minimal risk. General-purpose AI models carry their own obligations.
NIST AI RMF is voluntary and has four functions: Govern (cross-cutting), Map, Measure, Manage.
ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable AI management system standard. GDPR adds lawful basis requirements and limits on solely automated decisions.

AI governance differs from IT governance because behavior is probabilistic, changes over time and raises ethical questions. A centralized use-case inventory and defined roles (Chief AI Officer, AI ethics officer, AI champions) anchor it.
traps: Calling the NIST AI RMF certifiable. ISO/IEC 42001 is the certifiable one.
lessons.tip: When asked for the first governance step, an inventory of AI use cases is usually the answer.

lessons.summary: Responsible AI turns principles into measurable checks, especially for bias across groups.
points: Core principles: fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security, inclusiveness, transparency, accountability.
Bias comes from historical data, sampling, labeling and proxy variables that stand in for protected attributes.
Fairness metrics such as demographic parity, equal opportunity and equalized odds can conflict; choose based on context and document why.
Explainability can be global (how the model behaves overall) or local (why this decision). Consider energy use and societal impacts too.
traps: Assuming that removing a protected attribute removes bias. Proxies such as ZIP code can carry it.
lessons.tip: Fairness is demonstrated by testing outcomes across groups, not by intent.

lessons.summary: AI risk management sizes controls to impact, then keeps reassessing because models and data change.
points: Map each use case to its potential harms, then estimate likelihood and impact. Blast radius grows with autonomy and connected systems.
Risk tiers combine human impact with technical complexity and drive how much testing and oversight is required.
Treatments are mitigate, transfer, avoid or accept. Acceptance must be documented by an owner with authority.
Reassessment triggers include model updates, drift, new vulnerabilities, new data sources, new uses and incidents.
traps: Letting a technical team accept business risk. The accountable business owner accepts it.
lessons.tip: Tier first, then apply proportional controls.

lessons.summary: Data obligations follow data into models, and public availability does not equal permission.
points: Regulated types include PII, PHI, financial data and export-controlled data.
Training data raises licensing, copyright and fair-use questions that remain legally unsettled in many places.
Regulatory contamination: once regulated data enters a dataset or model, obligations can extend to the whole artifact.
Set retention and deletion schedules, and capture consent or another lawful basis at collection.
traps: Assuming scraped public data is free to use for training.
lessons.tip: Classify data before it enters the pipeline; it is far harder to remove afterwards.

lessons.summary: Outsourcing AI moves work to a provider but not accountability. Contracts and evidence carry the weight.
points: Due diligence: SOC 2 or ISO 27001/42001 evidence, model documentation, data usage terms (does the provider train on your data?), subprocessors.
Contract terms: security SLAs, incident notification with defined timelines, audit rights, data deletion on exit.
Track dependencies with an SBOM and an AIBOM covering models and datasets.
Shared responsibility: the provider secures the platform and model; you secure your data, access, prompts and usage. TEEs and confidential computing protect data in use.
traps: Believing a vendor contract transfers accountability for outcomes.
lessons.tip: Always check whether the provider can use your prompts or data for training.

lessons.summary: Oversight means named people with real authority to stop, override and sign off, backed by records.
points: Human-in-the-loop approves before an action takes effect. Human-on-the-loop monitors and can intervene. Human-out-of-the-loop has no real-time oversight.
Define who can intervene, override and sign off, by role.
Manage shadow AI with detection (proxy, CASB, expense data) plus approved alternatives and a clear policy.
Keep governance artifacts: model documentation, decision logs, exception records. Label synthetic content and deepfakes. Audit for compliance, bias, drift and outcomes.
traps: Banning AI outright as the shadow AI fix. It drives usage underground.
lessons.tip: If the question asks who can stop the system, the answer is a named role with documented authority.

lessons.summary: Training works when it is role-based and measured by behavior, not attendance.
points: Start with skills assessments and gap analyses for people who build, run or rely on AI.
Tailor content: developers need secure integration, operators need incident handling, executives need risk decisions, all users need acceptable use and data handling.
Measure effectiveness through behavior: fewer policy violations, more reported issues, better test results.
Build a risk-aware culture where people raise AI concerns early.
traps: Using completion rates as proof that training works.
lessons.tip: Role-based beats one-size-fits-all on this exam.

lessons.summary: Data governance assigns accountability and makes data traceable from source to model.
points: The owner is accountable and classifies data. The steward manages quality and day-to-day use. The custodian implements controls. Under GDPR, the controller decides purposes and the processor acts on instructions.
Sovereignty and residency rules limit where data and models may be stored or processed.
Classification tags should follow data into derived datasets, embeddings and models. Mark synthetic data distinctly from real data.
Chain of custody records who handled data and when, with integrity checks. The lifecycle runs from collection through validation, transformation, retention, archiving and deletion.
traps: Confusing the owner (accountable) with the custodian (implements).
lessons.tip: Lineage is what lets you scope an incident or honor an erasure request.

lessons.summary: Privacy controls start with collecting less and using it only for its stated purpose.
points: Privacy by Design: consent, purpose limitation, lawful use and data minimization from the start.
True anonymization is irreversible; pseudonymization and tokenization can be reversed. Differential privacy adds noise under a privacy budget, where a smaller epsilon means stronger privacy.
GDPR covers personal data of people in the EU. HIPAA covers PHI with business associate agreements. PCI DSS covers cardholder data, which should stay out of prompts and training.
Erasure is hard once data has shaped model weights; plan for unlearning or retraining.
traps: Treating tokenized data as anonymous. Anyone with the vault can reverse it.
lessons.tip: When in doubt, minimization is the first control.

lessons.summary: Training data is an attack surface. Protect its integrity and keep versions you can roll back to.
points: Integrity controls: access control on datasets, hashes, signed versions and validation before training.
Poisoning can degrade overall accuracy or plant targeted backdoors triggered by specific inputs. Clean-label attacks look correctly labeled.
Unauthorized label modification (label flipping) and malicious public datasets are common vectors. Versioning lets you identify and restore a clean set.
Training repeatedly on synthetic or AI-generated data risks collapse; verify synthetic data quality. Models can also memorize and leak training records.
traps: Assuming high test accuracy rules out a backdoor.
lessons.tip: Validate provenance before training, not after deployment.

lessons.summary: Protect AI data in every state, manage keys carefully and sanitize storage properly when it is retired.
points: DSPM discovers and classifies data across cloud stores, including vector databases and training buckets.
DLP and semantic filtering inspect prompts and outputs by meaning, not just patterns.
Encrypt at rest, in transit and in use (TEEs, confidential computing). Manage keys with KMS, BYOK where needed, rotation and separation of duties; keep secrets in a vault.

Purpose-based access and agentic data catalogs limit what each agent can reach. Sanitize media with cryptographic erasure when you can't destroy drives, or physical destruction such as shredding when you can.
traps: Treating file deletion as sanitization.
lessons.tip: Cloud or high-density storage you can't touch: cryptographic erasure.

lessons.summary: Model governance controls which models run, who owns them and how they change.
points: Every model needs an owner, a risk classification and an approval workflow.
Model cards document intended use, limitations, data and evaluation. Only models in the approved registry should deploy.
Secure the deployment pipeline: validation, packaging, serving and credential management. Sanitize inputs and outputs, and keep tested update and rollback procedures.
Monitor for drift, bias and anomalies, and keep privacy-preserving audit trails of data events.
traps: Allowing a model outside the approved registry into production.
lessons.tip: The registry is the source of truth for what is allowed to run.

lessons.summary: Apply the CIA triad to the model itself: its weights, its behavior and its uptime.
points: Confidentiality: restrict and log access to weights, encrypt them and protect proprietary algorithms.
Extraction prevention: rate limits, quotas, monitoring for systematic query patterns and limiting output detail such as confidence scores.
Watermarking marks outputs or models; fingerprinting proves ownership. Integrity relies on signing, hashing and version control.
Availability: rate limiting, quota enforcement and graceful degradation.
traps: Thinking encryption at rest stops extraction through the API.
lessons.tip: Large volumes of systematic, varied queries point to model extraction.

lessons.summary: Models and datasets you didn't build carry risks you can't see. Verify before you trust.
points: Public and third-party datasets can carry poisoning, PII and licensing problems.
Pre-trained and foundation models can hide backdoors, and some file formats execute code when loaded.
Verify provenance and authenticity with hashes, signatures and trusted registries.
Assess vendors on how they source, train and secure what they provide.
traps: Assuming a popular model on a public hub is safe.
lessons.tip: Safe serialization formats, scanning and hash or signature checks before loading.

lessons.summary: Design AI systems so that every boundary crossing is a checkpoint, especially tools and retrieved content.
points: Apply Zero Trust, defense in depth, Privacy by Design and secure defaults.
Threat model each component: prompt handling, retriever, vector database, model, tools and outputs.
Weigh trade-offs among latency, explainability and cost. Build versus buy turns on control, residency, skills and cost.
For MCP and agent-to-agent integrations: authenticate servers, allowlist and pin versions, give tools least privilege and treat tool output and descriptions as untrusted.
traps: Forgetting that tool descriptions are model input and can carry injected instructions.
lessons.tip: Every trust boundary needs authentication and authorization outside the model.

lessons.summary: Infrastructure for AI needs the usual hardening plus isolation for untrusted workloads and attention to physical demands.
points: Harden cloud, on-premises and hybrid deployments with baselines, private endpoints and least-privilege service accounts.
Isolate and sandbox training and inference. Model-generated code runs in sandboxes without default network egress.
Control resource exhaustion with rate limiting and compute throttling. Dedicated accelerator capacity avoids noisy neighbors and side channels.
Physical and environmental security matters: GPU density drives power and cooling needs, plus rack security and fire suppression.
traps: Skipping physical and environmental controls. They are explicitly in the outline.
lessons.tip: Untrusted code goes in a sandbox with no egress and no secrets.

lessons.summary: The MLOps pipeline can ship a poisoned model as easily as a good one, so gate it.
points: Secure CI/CD: signed artifacts, scanned containers and least-privilege pipeline credentials.
Protect ingestion and transformation with integrity checks and schema validation.
Track lineage for fine-tuning: which data produced which adapter or model version.
Use validation checkpoints and gates before promotion, and keep the ability to unlearn or retrain without specific data.
traps: Overlooking pipeline credentials, which are a prime target.
lessons.tip: A gate combines automated tests with an approval.

lessons.summary: Guardrails belong in the architecture: filter what goes in and out, and constrain what agents can do.
points: Sanitize prompts, filter content and validate context boundaries so retrieved text is treated as data, not instructions.
An orchestration layer or harness enforces allowed actions, step limits and approvals for autonomous behavior.
Test functionality, performance and load.
Stress test and validate exception handling so failures are safe.
traps: Relying on guardrails inside the model alone.
lessons.tip: High-risk actions should fail closed.

lessons.summary: Agents and workloads need their own identities so every action can be attributed.
points: Classify identities as human or non-human: workloads, agents, services and tools.
Unique identity per agent supports non-repudiation and accountability.
Machine-to-machine authentication uses OAuth client credentials, mutual TLS, workload identity federation and short-lived tokens. Humans use federation, SSO and MFA.
Keep secrets in a vault, never in prompts or code.
traps: Sharing one API key across agents. It destroys accountability.
lessons.tip: An agent acting for a user gets delegated, scoped tokens, not the user's full rights.

lessons.summary: Give each model and agent the least access it needs, for the least time, and limit what it can do on its own.
points: Apply least privilege and separation of duties across models and agentic workflows.
RBAC grants by role, ABAC by attributes and context, PBAC through a central policy engine. Just-in-time access removes standing privilege.
Set execution boundaries and narrow API scopes.
Prevent excessive agency (too much functionality, permission or autonomy), over-delegation and lateral movement between agents.
traps: Letting an agent inherit its user's full permissions.
lessons.tip: Split read and write tools; require approval for irreversible actions.

lessons.summary: Identities pile up as AI projects grow. Inventory them, review them and remove what's unused.
points: Maintain inventories of human and non-human identities.
Provision with an owner, and deprovision when projects end to avoid orphaned agent credentials.
Run periodic access reviews and use identity security posture management.
Audit resource use: token accounting, rate limits and session time-outs.
traps: Leaving agent credentials active after the project that needed them ends.
lessons.tip: Every identity, human or not, needs an owner.

lessons.summary: Operational readiness means clear roles, release criteria and rehearsed playbooks before anything goes wrong.
points: Apply least privilege and separation of duties in AI operations.
Define roles such as model owner, data owner, MLOps and SecOps.
Release requirements include human override baselines and reject-rate thresholds that trigger review.
Rehearse playbooks with tabletops (poisoning, tampering). Treat prompts, model versions and guardrail settings as configuration items and track drift.
traps: Forgetting that system prompts and guardrail settings are configuration items.
lessons.tip: Tabletop exercises validate playbooks across disciplines.

lessons.summary: You can't investigate what you didn't log. AI telemetry centers on the interaction trail.
points: Collect prompts, completions, retrieved content, embeddings, tool calls and API traffic.
Correlate AI events in SIEM and SOAR with threat intelligence, linked by session.
Protect log integrity (write-once storage, hashing) and document evidence.
Mask sensitive data in telemetry and monitor behavior, drift and agent actions in real time.
traps: Dropping prompt logs for privacy. Mask them instead; you need the evidence.
lessons.tip: The session ID is what ties a prompt to the tool call it caused.

lessons.summary: Runtime detection watches inputs, retrieval, outputs and resource use for signs of misuse.
points: Detect threats across inputs, retrieval chains, outputs and resource consumption.
Watch for unauthorized identities and over-privileged agents.
Flag secrets in outputs and anomalous tool use: unusual tools, parameters or frequency.
Monitor integrity of data, knowledge bases, models and pipelines. AI-driven SecOps (UEBA, triage, hunting) helps at scale.
traps: Ignoring token usage spikes, which can signal abuse or exhaustion attacks.
lessons.tip: Baseline normal agent behavior so deviations stand out.

lessons.summary: Track AI weaknesses like any other vulnerabilities, but prioritize by context and accept that some can't be patched.
points: Keep a register of model vulnerabilities and exposures, including framework CVEs and jailbreak susceptibility.
Prioritize by exposure and consequence, not severity scores alone.
Patch pipelines, dependencies and open-source components.
Legacy models get compensating controls and strict usage limits until retirement; measure posture continuously.
traps: Assuming every model weakness has a patch.
lessons.tip: Exposure plus business impact sets priority.

lessons.summary: Contain first, preserve evidence, then involve the right disciplines.
points: Classify incidents: prompt injection, jailbreak, poisoning, model theft and others.
Escalate across SecOps, MLOps, data science, legal and compliance, since notification duties may apply.
Contain with rollback, endpoint isolation, rate limits, disabled tools and revoked credentials. Suspend pipelines and terminate agents when needed.
Preserve weights, configurations, prompts, dataset snapshots and logs before rollback or deletion.
traps: Rolling back before preserving the suspect model as evidence.
lessons.tip: Active harm: stop it first, then investigate.

lessons.summary: Find the root cause, remove it fully and prove the system is safe before it returns.
points: Reconstruct the kill chain, for example from poisoned data or untrusted tool output.
Perform root cause analysis with a forensic timeline.
Attribution is often hard and isn't required to eradicate.
Eradicate by sanitizing data, retraining, patching or rebuilding stores, then run safety regression tests before reintroduction.
traps: Retraining on data that hasn't been sanitized, which reintroduces the poison.
lessons.tip: Fix the root cause, not the symptom.

lessons.summary: Recovery restores trusted states, keeps the business running without AI if needed and feeds lessons back.
points: Recover with trusted model rollback, clean checkpoints and vector-store restoration from verified backups.
A circuit breaker stops a system automatically when a threshold is crossed; a kill switch is usually a stop that a person triggers.
BC/DR plans map critical AI dependencies, including outside model providers, and define fallback modes.
Hold post-incident reviews and update the TTP register. Decommission securely: delete weights, revoke keys and identities, unlearn where needed.
traps: Restoring from backups without verifying their integrity.
lessons.tip: Know the fallback when the AI is unavailable.

lessons.summary: Choose the threat modeling method that fits the system, then cover every component and actor.
points: STRIDE classifies threats by type. PASTA is a seven-stage, risk-centric method tied to business impact. MAESTRO is built for agentic and multi-agent systems.
Threat actors include outsiders, insiders and compromised non-human agents.
Adversarial ML attacks: evasion, poisoning, extraction, inversion, backdoors and membership inference.
GenAI, RAG, agentic and multimodal systems add threats such as instructions hidden in images. Availability attacks exhaust compute or tokens.
traps: Choosing STRIDE when the question emphasizes agentic or multi-agent systems; MAESTRO fits better.
lessons.tip: Threat model at each trust boundary.

lessons.summary: Bring change control to everything that changes model behavior, not just code.
points: Integrate security across data collection, training, evaluation, deployment and monitoring.
Separate environments, apply least privilege and secure API integration.
Version models, datasets, prompts and retrieval indexes.
Use staged rollouts (canary, blue/green, shadow) with defined rollback.
traps: Treating a prompt change as too small for change control.
lessons.tip: Version everything that can change behavior.

lessons.summary: Procurement is a security control: check vendors, licenses and the authenticity of what you receive.
points: Assess vendors through certifications, assessment reports and testing results.
Settle data ownership, licensing and legal terms before acquisition.
Verify pedigree with cryptographic hashes and digital signatures.
Maintain an AI-BOM for hardware, software and data dependencies.
traps: Assuming open-weight models allow any use. Licenses vary and some restrict commercial use.
lessons.tip: Verify signatures before trust.

lessons.summary: AI testing starts with authorization and scope, then targets the paths attackers use.
points: Define scope, objectives, scenarios, rules of engagement and written authorization.
Test GenAI, RAG and agentic systems for direct and indirect injection, jailbreaks, data leakage, retrieval poisoning, tool abuse and excessive agency.
Use threat-informed red teaming that combines manual and automated testing.
AI-assisted tools can generate attacks and explore novel paths at scale.
traps: Starting tests before written authorization and scope are agreed.
lessons.tip: Include indirect injection through every data source the system reads.

lessons.summary: Good findings are triaged, mapped, reproducible and explained to each audience.
points: Triage by severity, exploitability, reproducibility and business impact. Report success rates over repeated attempts because LLMs are non-deterministic.
Separate security vulnerabilities from model limitations such as hallucinations.
Map findings to MITRE ATLAS and the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications.
Document evidence and reproduction steps, and tailor communication for technical and non-technical stakeholders.
traps: Dismissing a finding because it doesn't reproduce every time.
lessons.tip: Executives need business impact; engineers need reproduction steps.

lessons.summary: A mitigation isn't done until it is prioritized, implemented, validated and monitored.
points: Targeted mitigations include adversarial training, provenance tracking and data validation.
General controls include filtering, sandboxing, rate limiting and watermarking.
Prioritize by risk, feasibility and business context.
Validate with regression testing and keep monitoring residual risk.
traps: Declaring a fix complete without regression testing.
lessons.tip: Regression test both the fix and the safety behavior you already had.

flashcards.front: Labeled training data, predicting a category
flashcards.back: Supervised learning (classification).
Transformers, which use attention to weigh relationships between tokens.

traps.title: The system prompt is not a control
traps.body: Answers that rely on telling the model to behave are almost always wrong when a deterministic control is offered: authorization, filtering, scoping or isolation.

traps.title: Contain before you investigate
traps.body: When harm is ongoing, stop it first: halt the agent, revoke access, isolate. Root cause analysis comes after.

traps.title: Preserve before you roll back
traps.body: Rollback or deletion can destroy evidence. Capture weights, configuration, datasets and logs first.

traps.title: Authorize before retrieval
traps.body: In RAG, filter documents by the user's permissions before they enter the context. Once inside, prompts can't keep them out.

traps.title: Limitation or vulnerability?
traps.body: A hallucination with no security impact is a reliability finding, not a vulnerability. Check whether a boundary was crossed.

traps.title: Training time or inference time?
traps.body: Poisoning and backdoors happen in training. Evasion, injection and extraction happen at inference. Placing the attack in time usually identifies it.

traps.title: Accountability doesn't transfer
traps.body: Using a vendor or hosted model never moves accountability for outcomes off the deploying organization.

traps.title: Inventory comes first
traps.body: For a new governance program or unclear AI exposure, the first step is usually finding out what AI is in use.

traps.title: Bans don't fix shadow AI
traps.body: The best answer pairs an approved tool and policy with detection, not a blanket ban or discipline alone.

traps.title: Changes trigger reassessment
traps.body: A model swap, update, new data source or drift means re-validating risk, even if the vendor made the change.

traps.title: Least privilege for agents
traps.body: Agents shouldn't inherit a user's full rights. Scope tools to the task and require approval for irreversible actions.

traps.title: Think like a manager
traps.body: ISC2 exams such as the CISSP are widely described as rewarding a manager's perspective. Expect similar judgment questions here, though ISC2 hasn't published the pilot's style: favor answers that address risk through process, governance and the right roles over a single quick technical fix, unless the scenario is an active incident.
